article_title: The Rise of AI Shopping Assistants: Fashion’s Smartest Stylists
sub_title: AI shopping assistants use conversational intelligence, behavioural learning, and contextual understanding to interpret user intent and offer highly personalised suggestions. Unlike basic recommendation algorithms, they engage in natural language dialogue, adapt over time, and respond to changing style needs and real-time preferences. While they are most visible in digital commerce, their influence extends to physical retail through virtual try-ons, connected store experiences, and real-time inv
article_content: The fashion industry stands at the intersection of creativity and technology, where digital innovation is no longer a backstage function but a front-row driver of consumer experience. Among the most transformative developments is the rise of AI shopping assistants—intelligent systems that guide, personalise, and even execute purchasing decisions on behalf of users. These agents are redefining the traditional retail model by offering real-time recommendations, understanding nuanced preferences, and facilitating seamless transactions across platforms. As fashion consumers increasingly seek convenience, personalisation, and relevance, AI assistants are stepping in as digital stylists, curators, and concierges. Their ability to interpret natural language, analyse behavioural data, and respond with tailored product suggestions is reshaping how brands engage with audiences. From luxury e-commerce to fast fashion apps, AI is becoming a strategic asset, not just for operational efficiency, but for emotional resonance and brand loyalty. This article explores the emergence of AI shopping assistants in fashion retail, their technological foundations, market impact, and the evolving role they play in shaping consumer behaviour and brand strategy. How AI Shopping Assistants Work in Fashion AI shopping assistants in fashion operate through a sophisticated blend of machine learning, Natural Language Processing (NLP), and real-time data integration. These systems are engineered to interpret user intent, analyse preferences, and deliver personalised product recommendations with remarkable precision. At the core of their functionality is Natural Language understanding, which enables users to interact conversationally by describing occasions, style preferences, budgets, or even emotional tones. For instance, a user might say, “I’m looking for a confident, minimalist outfit for a pitch meeting,” and the assistant will parse this input to suggest tailored options that match both aesthetic and functional criteria. These assistants leverage user data and behavioural analytics, including past purchases, browsing history, saved items, and even social media engagement, to build dynamic style profiles. Advanced systems also incorporate visual recognition and image-based search, allowing users to upload photos or screenshots and receive similar product suggestions across brands and price points. On the backend, AI agents integrate with retail databases, inventory systems, and e-commerce platforms, ensuring that recommendations reflect real-time availability, sizing, and shipping options. Some assistants are further enhanced by collaborative filtering algorithms, which compare user behaviour with similar profiles to surface trending or complementary items. In fashion-specific contexts, AI assistants are trained on style taxonomies, seasonal trends, and brand-specific nuances, enabling them to distinguish between “boho chic” and “urban minimalist,” or to recommend fabrics suitable for tropical climates versus winter layering. Ultimately, these systems function as intelligent intermediaries between consumers and fashion ecosystems, streamlining discovery, enhancing decision-making, and elevating the overall shopping experience. How AI Is Powering Personalised Shopping Forget endless scrolling and clunky filters. Today’s shoppers are engaging with AI assistants through natural language by asking questions, describing occasions, and receiving curated suggestions in seconds. Personalisation has become a cornerstone of modern fashion retail, and artificial intelligence is now the engine driving it forward. By leveraging Conversational AI and Generative AI, brands are able to deliver tailored experiences that reflect individual preferences, behaviours, and contexts—at scale. Conversational AI Conversational AI enables users to interact with shopping platforms through natural language, transforming static search into dynamic dialogue. These systems use advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) to interpret queries that go beyond keywords—capturing tone, intent, and emotional nuance. For example, a user might say: “I’m looking for something elegant but low-maintenance for a business trip to Singapore.” Rather than returning generic results, the AI assistant understands the occasion, climate, and style preference, and recommends breathable, wrinkle-resistant garments in a refined aesthetic. It may also suggest complementary accessories, travel-friendly footwear, and local store availability. Generative AI Generative AI adds a creative layer to personalisation by producing original content, ranging from product descriptions and styling tips to personalised lookbooks and outfit combinations. These models analyse user data, fashion trends, and brand aesthetics to generate recommendations that feel bespoke. In fashion retail, Generative AI can: Together, Conversational and Generative AI form a powerful ecosystem that transforms shopping from a transactional activity into a personalised journey. They enable brands to move beyond segmentation towards true individualisation, where every interaction feels relevant, responsive, and emotionally resonant. The Numbers: Why Fashion Cannot Ignore AI The adoption of AI shopping assistants in fashion is no longer a futuristic concept. It is a present-day imperative backed by compelling data. As of 2025, 43 per cent of US adults are aware of AI shopping assistants, with Gen Z and millennials leading the charge in usage. 1 These intelligent agents are proving their worth by reducing decision-making time by up to 60 per cent, according to Capgemini, and boosting conversion rates by 30–50 per cent when integrated into the shopping journey. Retailers leveraging AI assistants also report a 20 per cent increase in average order value, thanks to smarter upselling and personalised bundling. With the global market for AI shopping assistants projected to reach $22.1 billion by 2032, 2 fashion brands that ignore this shift risk falling behind in both customer engagement and revenue growth. article_content: In fashion, the right accessories can make or break a look. The same is true for the supply chain. For years, many fashion brands relied on a single sourcing country because it was efficient, cost-effective, and predictable. China was the go-to choice, offering scale, expertise, and speed. However, that ‘single-source’ strategy has transformed into a single point of failure. Concentrated supply chains are nothing more than concentrated risks. From pandemic-era shutdowns to blocked shipping lanes to volatile tariffs, global disruptions have shown how fragile single-region sourcing really is. The result is delayed collections, empty shelves, and lost revenue. For fashion brands that live and die by seasonality, these disruptions are devastating. That is why supplier diversification has gone from a nice-to-have to a must-have. It is no longer optional for sourcing, buying, and supply chain teams to rely on a narrow set of suppliers. Diversification is now a key pillar of supply chain resilience, helping to protect margins, preserve brand reputation, and keep products flowing to market on time. Why Fashion is Removing Beyond One-Stop Sourcing The numbers always tell a story, and McKinsey found that only 2 per cent of companies have visibility beyond their tier-two suppliers. That means most brands have no idea where their fabrics are woven or where their trims are coming from until something goes wrong. This blind spot often leads to material shortages, compliance issues, and missed deliveries that can wipe out margins and erode customer trust. Forward-thinking businesses are already rewriting the rules. Look at Shein, which recently partnered with Reliance Retail in India. The fast-fashion powerhouse plans to grow its network of Indian suppliers from 150 factories to 1,000 in a single year and start exporting India-made apparel to the US and UK. Shein is not just diversifying to avoid tariffs, it is building speed and flexibility into its supply chain by spreading production across multiple regions. Even more impressive is how Shein pairs this strategy with data-driven agility. Each new design starts with a tiny production run of just 100 pieces. Only the winners get scaled up. This ‘test and react’ model allows Shein to meet consumer demand without overproducing, a playbook that any fashion brand can attempt to replicate. Balancing Cost, Risk, and Responsibility Of course, diversification is not simply about finding cheaper factories, but it involves striking the right balance: The Shein-Reliance partnership also highlights an important point that diversification sometimes requires helping suppliers level up. Whether that means upgrading equipment, sourcing specialty fabrics, or investing in training, supplier development is often part of the journey. Tech as a Secret Weapon Mapping a global supply base manually is like trying to untangle a knot of necklaces. This is where technology becomes fashion’s best friend. Southeast Asia, especially Vietnam and Indonesia, is emerging as a cost-competitive alternative to China. Nearshoring is also gaining momentum. US retailers are exploring Mexico and Central America while European brands look to Türkiye, Portugal, and North Africa to stay closer to their customers and shorten lead times. This shift will not happen overnight, but the winners will be the brands that start now. article_content: The textile and apparel industry represents one of the largest global manufacturing sectors, providing employment to millions and contributing significantly to international trade. Its value chain extends from fibre cultivation and yarn production to fabric construction, apparel design, retailing, and end-of-life management. As consumer expectations evolve and global competition intensifies, the industry faces increasing pressure to reduce costs, improve quality, minimise waste, and accelerate product development. Growing awareness of sustainability has also resulted in heightened demand for traceable and ethical supply chains. Industry 4.0, characterised by cyber-physical systems, IoT connectivity, automation, and pervasive digitisation, positions big data analytics as a transformative force in textile manufacturing. Factories now utilise continuous data streams from machines, enterprise systems, logistics networks, and consumer platforms to enable real-time, predictive decision-making. This represents a fundamental shift from traditional production practices, which relied largely on manual control and experience-based adjustments. The adoption of big data in textiles thus signifies a broader rethinking of production strategies, supply chain models, and sustainability frameworks. This article provides an expanded overview of the role of big data in reshaping the textile and apparel industry and outlines future research directions and industrial opportunities. Defining Big Data in the Textile Context Big data encompasses datasets that exceed the capacity of conventional software tools to collect, store, process, and analyse. In textiles, such data originates from numerous interconnected sources across the production lifecycle. Here, it is pertinent to mention the four Vs of big data. Volume : Modern textile production generates extremely large volumes of data. Spinning machines, for example, record spindle speed, twist levels, temperature, and yarn breakages. Dyeing and finishing operations document chemical concentrations, colour measurements, and bath parameters, while retail platforms accumulate millions of transactional records. Velocity : High-speed textile operations require rapid data acquisition and processing. IoT-enabled looms measure vibration and tension in real time, RFID-based logistics platforms monitor material movement across borders, and online consumer behaviour continuously updates trend forecasts. Variety : The industry generates structured data such as ERP logs, semi-structured data such as sensor reports, and unstructured data such as defect images, social media content, and videos. Such diversity demands adaptable database systems and advanced analytics. Veracity : Data reliability fluctuates due to raw material variations, sensor inaccuracies, operator errors, and inconsistent consumer input. Ensuring data validity is essential for accurate predictive modelling. Big Data Architecture in the Textile and Apparel Industry Big data architecture describes how information is collected, transmitted, stored, processed, and visualised. Data Sources : Manufacturing equipment provides continuous operational data, including spindle and loom behaviour, dye uptake levels, and chemical dosing patterns. Image and video systems capture fabric surfaces for defect detection and stitching quality inspection. Supply chains generate tracking data through RFID tags, QR codes, telematics, warehouse systems, and GPS. Market and consumer analytics originate from e-commerce portals, loyalty programmes, and social media content. Environmental monitoring systems track resource consumption, emissions, and waste. Data Storage and Computing Technologies : Cloud platforms such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud ensure scalable storage and accessibility. Distributed systems like Hadoop HDFS manage massive datasets, while NoSQL databases support semi-structured and unstructured data. Real-time pipelines utilise technologies like Apache Kafka and Spark Streaming to process and analyse machine-generated data instantly. Analytics and Visualisation Tools : Machine learning frameworks, including TensorFlow, PyTorch, Scikit-learn, XGBoost, and LightGBM, support deep learning models for defect detection and predictive maintenance. Visualisation platforms like Tableau, Power BI, and QlikView enable real-time monitoring and decision-making. Statistical tools such as R and SAS provide regression modelling, clustering, and process optimisation capabilities. Applications of Big Data in Textiles and Apparel Manufacturing Process Optimisation : Big data analytics predicts yarn breakages using spindle temperature and tension data, adjusts loom settings automatically to minimise stoppages, optimises dye bath parameters to reduce chemical consumption, and identifies hidden bottlenecks through multivariate analysis. For instance, mills can proactively adjust environmental conditions when certain humidity levels are correlated with higher breakage rates. Quality Control and Smart Inspection Systems : Automated vision systems capture continuous fabric images, while deep learning models detect defects such as holes, stains, mispicks, and slubs. These systems relate defect patterns to machine settings, operator behaviour, or ambient conditions. Automated inspection improves reliability and accelerates quality assessment. Supply Chain Optimisation : Big data supports traceability from raw fibre to finished apparel, predicts shipment delays, enhances demand forecasting, and evaluates supplier performance based on delivery times and defect rates. Such transparency minimises lead times, reduces risk, and supports compliance. Retail Analytics and Consumer Insights : Retailers use big data to analyse social media sentiment, predict style and colour trends, personalise product recommendations, and implement dynamic pricing. These insights increase profitability and consumer satisfaction. Smart Textiles and Wearable Data Streams : Wearable textiles equipped with sensors generate physiological, biomechanical, and environmental data. This information supports medical monitoring, athletic performance assessment, occupational safety, and military operations. Integration with mobile and cloud platforms enables continuous real-time analytics. Sustainability and Circular Economy : Big data monitors water, chemical, and energy usage, tracks waste in cutting rooms, optimises recycling flows, and evaluates the environmental footprint across product lifecycles. These insights contribute to environmentally responsible manufacturing. Case Studies Predictive Maintenance in Spinning Mills : IoT sensors monitor vibration, sound, and temperature to predict spindle and bearing failures weeks in advance, reducing downtime and extending equipment life. Trend Forecasting in Fast Fashion : Fast-fashion brands analyse millions of social media posts, images, and search queries to identify emerging trends, reducing the lead time between concept and market introduction. Dyehouse Optimisation Using Big Data : Machine learning in dyehouses improves colour consistency, reduces chemical usage by up to 20 per cent, and lowers water consumption by 10 to 15 per cent. Challenges and Limitations Data quality issues arise from inconsistent formats across machines and suppliers. High implementation costs hinder smaller enterprises. Skill shortages persist due to the industry’s traditional reliance on manual expertise. Legacy machinery lacks digital connectivity, creating interoperability challenges. Privacy concerns grow as retail and wearable technologies collect sensitive consumer data. Future Research Directions Digital twins will simulate textile machines and factories to optimise operations before physical implementation. AI-integrated ecosystems will enable autonomous factories where machines self-adjust and supply chains self-coordinate. Blockchain will support transparent recording of fibre provenance and ethical practices. Circular textile systems will use data to identify recyclable materials and optimise fibre recovery processes. Edge computing will allow machines to process data locally with minimal latency. Big data analytics has become essential to the modern textile and apparel industry. It enhances productivity, quality, transparency, sustainability, and consumer engagement. Although challenges related to data integration, workforce skills, and infrastructure remain, continuing digitalisation ensures that data-driven operations will define the sector’s future. Technologies such as digital twins, blockchain, AI, and edge computing will further transform the industry into a smarter, more sustainable, and interconnected system. These insights help improve sales, reduce returns, and align collections with real demand. article_content: Fashion has always been about more than just clothing. It has been a reflection of culture, innovation, and identity. Today, textiles are stepping into an entirely new role: becoming the foundation of wearable technology. No longer limited to aesthetics or comfort, fabrics are being engineered to sense, respond, and even communicate. From yoga pants that track muscle activity to hospital gowns that monitor vital signs, textiles are transforming everyday garments into intelligent companions. This fusion of fashion and function is not just futuristic; it is happening now. The global smart textiles market is expected to expand significantly, rising from $6.61 billion in 2025 to $67.62 billion by 2035. 1 Designers and technologists are working hand in hand to redefine what people wear and why they wear it. The result? Clothing that does not just look good, but also actively enhances health, performance, and lifestyle. From Fabric to Function Traditionally, textiles have been valued for their comfort, durability, and aesthetic appeal. Today, they are evolving into smart textiles, i.e., materials embedded with sensors, conductive fibres, and responsive coatings that allow clothing to interact with the wearer and the environment. This shift is transforming garments from passive fashion items into active devices capable of monitoring health, enhancing performance, and even generating energy. But what does this transformation really look like? Market Growth and Potential The global smart textiles market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 32.45 per cent from 2025 to 2035 2 driven by consumer demand and technological breakthroughs. These figure highlights how textiles are becoming central to the wearable revolution, not just an accessory to electronics. According to recent reports, nearly 30 per cent of wearable technology innovations now involve textile integration, highlighting how fabrics are becoming the preferred medium for embedding intelligence. The healthcare sector alone accounts for over 40 per cent of smart textile applications, underscoring their role in patient monitoring and preventive care. This evolution is not just technical; it is also cultural. By embedding intelligence into fabrics, designers are redefining the very purpose of clothing. Garments are no longer static; they are dynamic systems that respond, adapt, and even communicate. In essence, textiles are becoming the interface between humans and technology, bridging fashion with function in ways that were once unimaginable. Applications Across Industries Healthcare Smart fabrics can monitor vital signs such as heart rate, temperature, and hydration. For example, hospital gowns embedded with sensors reduce the need for bulky monitoring equipment. These textiles are also being used in rehabilitation, where garments can track muscle recovery and provide feedback to patients and doctors. With the rise of telemedicine, smart clothing could become a bridge between patients and healthcare providers, offering continuous monitoring outside hospital walls. A notable case is Hexoskin, 3 a Canadian company whose biometric shirts record ECG, breathing rate, and activity levels, transmitting data to smartphones for continuous monitoring. Similarly, Sensoria 4 has developed smart socks that track foot pressure and gait, helping prevent injuries in diabetic patients. Sports and Fitness Athletic wear now integrates textiles that track muscle activity, posture, and performance, giving athletes real-time feedback. This allows coaches and trainers to fine-tune workouts and prevent injuries by spotting strain before it becomes serious. Smart fabrics can also measure sweat composition, helping athletes understand hydration and electrolyte levels during intense training. As fitness becomes increasingly data-driven, these textiles are turning everyday gear into personalised performance labs. Under Armour’s Athlete Recovery Sleepwear 5 , infused with bioceramic particles, reflects infrared energy back to the body to aid muscle recovery. Meanwhile, OMsignal 6 produces smart shirts that monitor breathing and heart rate during workouts, offering athletes data-driven insights. Fashion and Lifestyle Designers are experimenting with fabrics that change colour, light up, or adapt to temperature, merging creativity with utility. Imagine a dress that shifts hues depending on mood or environment, or jackets that warm up automatically in cold weather. These innovations are not only functional but also open new avenues for self-expression, making fashion more interactive and personalised. With sustainability in mind, some smart textiles are being designed to reduce energy consumption, aligning with eco-conscious consumer trends. Luxury brands are also exploring smart textiles, with Ralph Lauren’s PoloTech shirt 7 offering biometric tracking while maintaining a sleek fashion aesthetic. Military and Safety Textiles with built-in communication systems or protective layers enhance soldier safety and occupational performance. For instance, uniforms can be equipped with sensors that detect chemical exposure or monitor fatigue levels in real time. Firefighters and construction workers are also benefiting from smart fabrics such as smart jackets by Teijin 8 that regulate body temperature and provide alerts in hazardous conditions. These industries are improving safety standards while reducing reliance on external devices by embedding intelligence directly into clothing. Why Textiles Matter in Wearables Unlike rigid devices, textiles offer flexibility, breathability, and comfort, making them ideal for long-term use. A smartwatch may track steps, but a smart shirt can monitor multiple health metrics without disrupting daily life. Textiles also allow seamless integration of technology into everyday routines, turning clothing into invisible assistants rather than noticeable gadgets. Beyond comfort, textiles provide surface area and adaptability that rigid devices cannot. Fabrics can cover the entire body, enabling more comprehensive data collection and interaction. They also allow for discreet design, ensuring that technology blends into fashion rather than standing apart as a gadget. Importantly, smart textiles can be machine-washable and durable, making them practical for everyday wear. As sustainability becomes a priority, textiles offer the chance to embed intelligence into eco-friendly fibres, ensuring that innovation aligns with environmental responsibility. Innovations Driving Change Textiles are no longer passive materials; they are becoming active participants in wearable technology, shaping the future of fashion, healthcare, and beyond. With billions of dollars flowing into research and development, the next decade will see clothing that not only looks good but also thinks, feels, and responds. Designers are no longer limited to fabric as a canvas for aesthetics; they can now create garments that interact with the environment, adapt to the wearer’s needs, and express individuality in dynamic ways. In healthcare, smart textiles promise to reduce hospital costs by enabling remote patient monitoring, while in sports, they are redefining performance gear into personalised coaching tools. Eco-friendly smart fabrics are ensuring that innovation does not come at the cost of the planet. As consumers demand both technology and responsibility, the fusion of smart textiles with sustainable practices will set the tone for the future of fashion-tech. In short, textiles are becoming the interface between humans and technology. They are becoming a silent yet powerful medium that merges comfort, creativity, and connectivity. The next generation of clothing will not just be worn; it will be experienced. Unlike traditional wearables, the technology is integrated directly into the fabric. Many smart textiles are designed to be washable, flexible and suitable for everyday use. Technology advancements have made sensors and conductive fibres resistant to moisture, movement and detergents, although washing instructions often differ from standard garments. Healthcare and sports are leading adoption due to demand for continuous monitoring and performance insights. Fashion, defence, and safety sectors are also integrating smart fabrics for communication, protection, and enhanced functionality. Smart textiles are likely to complement and gradually replace certain forms of rigid wearables, especially where comfort and continuous monitoring are essential. article_content: Most people do not realise that the textile chemicals market has a much larger impact than just making fabrics. People’s thinking of textiles typically includes the final product including how it looks, feels, and is designed and they do not consider the role that the chemistry plays in creating these characteristics. Textile chemicals support the entire production process for many types of textiles, whether manufacturing consumer apparel on a daily basis or speciality industrial textiles, and assist manufacturers as they produce fabrics that are both performance-based and aesthetically pleasing. Fast fashion has led to an increase in the textile chemicals industry by encouraging manufacturers to utilise chemical products that enable them to create fast-paced production cycles with rapid design changes. These fast production cycles provide manufacturers with the opportunity to speed up the dyeing, finishing, and treatment processes without sacrificing quality. Another factor in the expansion of the textile chemicals sector is the technical textile market. Technical textiles are used in many applications such as healthcare, automotive, construction, and sports. The fabrics used in these applications must possess specific functional properties, such as flame retardancy, water resistance, or anti-microbial properties. All of these properties are heavily dependent on the use of textile chemicals. In the marketplace for textile chemicals, there are a variety of chemical applications related to the manufacturing of textiles. The first three categories of chemicals (i.e., pre-treatment chemicals, dyeing and printing chemicals, and finishing chemicals) are used during the first three stages of manufacturing textiles. Pre-treatment chemicals remove impurities such as dirt, grease/oil, and natural fibres from raw cotton to prepare it for processing into finished goods and to ensure its ability to absorb dye and finish. Dyeing and printing chemicals give textiles their colour and provide patterns for textiles by creating conditions that allow for uniform dye distribution and long-lasting colour retention of textiles even after many washes. Finishing chemicals create the final appearance of the textile product after the last stage of manufacturing. They can also modify the final appearance of textiles by applying various characteristics such as adding softness, wrinkle-resistance, water-resistance, and durability. The finished garments produced using each of the three types of finished textiles depend on the exact formulation of the chemicals used. Therefore, the quality of each of the individual chemicals used to make up the finished textile product affects the quality of the finished textile product. Innovation continues to influence the textile chemicals industry in many significant ways. Textile chemical manufacturers are developing their products to provide better performance with a lower environmental impact. One area of development is the creation of eco-friendly chemicals. There is a growing pressure to limit the use of harmful chemicals and replace them with less harmful ones, including low-impact dyes, biodegradable chemicals and water conservational solutions. Another area of development is performance enhancement. Manufacturers are developing new formulations to produce more functional fabrics. Examples include moisture-wicking finishes on activewear, antimicrobial treatment for health care textiles, and UV protection for outdoor fabrics. The textile chemicals market has been evolving due to changing expectations from both manufacturers and end users. A greater focus on sustainability has led brands to look for chemical products that meet environmental standards and offer reductions in water and energy consumed in production. As a result, suppliers have been forced to reconsider how their products are formulated and function. Additionally, consumers are becoming more curious about what is included in the products they buy. Interest in skin-friendly textiles, non-toxic treatments, and environmentally friendly production have increased dramatically over recent years. On the manufacturer side of the equation, there is a demand for consistency and efficiency. Manufacturers require chemicals that are predictable and have similar characteristics from batch-to-batch and from one environmental condition to another when they have high volumes of production. The textile chemicals industry has continued to experience steady growth. However, there are still a few issues within the industry that will remain ongoing challenges for the foreseeable future. First, environmental regulations are becoming more punitive, restricting how companies produce and use chemicals. Because of this, companies will have to keep investing in compliance, testing, and reformulating, which generally raise the cost of doing business. Second, there is an issue of raw materials. Many of these textile chemicals are derived from certain raw material inputs, and the fluctuation in the price of raw material inputs can negatively impact the price and production of textile chemicals. Third, companies have had challenges achieving a balance between performance and sustainability. In some cases, companies may produce high-performance chemicals, but they may not always meet environmental standards. Therefore, manufacturers are challenged to find alternatives without sacrificing performance. The evolution of the textile industry is directly tied to what happens in the textile chemical market in the years to come. Sustainability will continue to be paramount, creating an increase in demand for sustainable chemical solutions. Developments in chemical technology will include waterless dyeing technologies, energy-efficient processing, and biodegradable finishes, which are likely to reduce the environmental impact of textile manufacturing without sacrificing quality. As a result, there is an increasing emphasis on transparency in this market. Brands want to know exactly what chemical ingredients are used in the manufacture of their products, and how those chemicals will affect the environment. This is driving the textile chemicals industry towards more open supply chains that provide full traceability back through the supply chain. The textile chemicals market is set to remain a cornerstone of the textile value chain, underpinning both functionality and aesthetics. As the industry navigates evolving sustainability mandates, regulatory pressures, and shifting consumer expectations, innovation will be central to future growth. The transition towards eco-conscious formulations, improved efficiency, and greater transparency will not only redefine product development but also shape competitive advantage, ensuring long-term resilience and relevance in a rapidly transforming global textile landscape. Beyond aesthetics, texture establishes emotional connection. Soft knits suggest comfort and intimacy. Metallic fringe conveys glamour and energy. Raw edges imply rebellion and modernity. Through texture, designers tell stories without relying on overt branding. Fringe: From Subculture to Sophistication Fringe remains one of fashion’s most dynamic textured elements. Historically associated with indigenous craftsmanship, Western wear, and the flapper dresses of the 1920s, fringe has undergone multiple reinventions. It symbolised liberation during the Jazz Age, freedom during the bohemian movements of the 1960s and 1970s, and now sophistication in contemporary luxury fashion. Today, fringe appears in precision-cut leather strips, silk-thread tassels, metallic chains, and sustainable yarn alternatives. It is no longer confined to costume-like interpretations. Instead, it is refined, controlled, and strategically placed. Designers use fringe to introduce movement into structured silhouettes and to create layered depth without overwhelming the garment. Fringe succeeds because of its kinetic quality. It transforms stillness into drama. With each step, it animates the body. It also allows adaptability. A full-fringe skirt makes a bold statement, while a subtle hemline trim or sleeve accent adds controlled texture. In Indian and fusion fashion, fringe integrates seamlessly into sarees, dupattas, lehengas, and even contemporary menswear shawls, bridging heritage and modernity. Beyond Fringe: The Spectrum of Textured Details While fringe leads many conversations around texture, it is only one of many techniques shaping contemporary design. Pleating and smocking introduce structural texture. Pleats create architectural precision and rhythm within garments. Micro-pleats in lightweight fabrics produce fluid movement, while broader pleats in structured textiles create sculptural effects. Smocking, often executed by hand, combines elasticity with intricate detailing, offering both function and aesthetic appeal. Embroidery and appliqué remain foundational to textured fashion. Raised embroidery, three-dimensional floral motifs, beadwork, and layered appliqué techniques bring tactile richness to garments. In South Asian fashion particularly, embroidery is deeply rooted in heritage. Modern interpretations lean towards tonal embroidery for understated elegance, oversized motifs for contemporary impact, and mixed-material applications that combine organza, leather, metallic threads, and silk. Fabric manipulation offers another avenue for texture. Techniques such as ruching, quilting, gathering, folding, and draping generate dimension directly from the base textile. This approach often aligns with sustainability initiatives because it avoids excessive external embellishment. Instead, designers manipulate the inherent qualities of the fabric to create organic depth and visual interest. Texture and the Psychology of Luxury Luxury today extends beyond logos and brand visibility. It revolves around experience. Texture enhances that experience by increasing perceived value. Intricate surfaces suggest labour, skill, and intentional design. Consumers often associate detailed craftsmanship with premium pricing. Textured garments also enhance sensory engagement. Even in retail environments where touching merchandise may be limited, the visual suggestion of tactility invites curiosity. In digital marketing, close-up photography of embroidery, movement-focused videos of fringe, and detailed fabric shots elevate engagement and storytelling. In markets such as India’s growing bridge-to-luxury segment, textured detailing supports the demand for attainable glamour. Consumers seek pieces that feel elevated without being ostentatious. Texture offers sophistication without reliance on overt branding. Strategic Incorporation: A Professional Approach Incorporating textured details requires balance and clarity of design intent. Overuse can overwhelm the garment, while underuse may fail to create impact. Designers must begin with silhouette. If the cut is already complex, texture should be restrained. Conversely, minimalist silhouettes provide the perfect canvas for bold fringe, layered appliqué, or dramatic pleating. Fabric compatibility is essential. Lightweight chiffons demand delicate trims and lighter fringe. Structured satins and heavier silks can support denser embellishments. Placement determines effectiveness. Hemlines are ideal for movement-driven fringe. Sleeves add drama without overpowering the body. Bodices benefit from fine detailing rather than heavy layering. Accessories such as belts, bags, or capes allow experimentation without committing the entire garment to texture. Wearability remains a critical consideration. Texture must enhance rather than restrict movement. Weight, durability, and maintenance requirements directly influence commercial viability. Designers must account for production complexity, quality control, and packaging methods to protect embellished surfaces. Texture in Menswear Textured detailing is no longer confined to womenswear. Contemporary menswear increasingly embraces expressive surfaces. Fringed shawls layered over kurtas, subtly textured bandhgalas, quilted Nehru jackets, and tonal thread embroidery demonstrate a shift towards nuanced sophistication. Modern male consumers are more open to experimentation, particularly in occasion wear and fusion fashion. Sustainability and Craft Revival Many textured techniques rely on handwork, making them inherently supportive of artisan communities. Embroidery clusters, smocking specialists, pleating workshops, and weaving communities contribute to the richness of textured fashion. Designers who integrate these elements can simultaneously strengthen ethical positioning and preserve craft traditions. Sustainable approaches to texture include using upcycled yarns for fringe, implementing zero-waste fabric manipulation techniques, and emphasising hand-finishing processes within brand storytelling. When communicated effectively, these efforts enhance both aesthetic value and consumer trust. Styling Textured Garments For stylists and editors, textured garments require thoughtful coordination. Heavy fringe pairs best with clean silhouettes. Competing patterns can dilute impact. Texture should be allowed to remain the focal point, with minimal accessories and balanced colour palettes. In photography, directional lighting enhances depth, while motion shots amplify the dynamism of fringe and layered details. Commercial Outlook and Future Directions From a retail perspective, garments featuring visible detailing often justify higher price points due to perceived craftsmanship. Texture provides differentiation in crowded markets and enhances in-store appeal. However, brands must manage labour costs, ensure durability, and maintain consistent quality control to sustain profitability. Looking ahead, innovation continues to reshape textured fashion. Designers are experimenting with three-dimensional printed embellishments, laser-cut fringe alternatives, bio-fabric tassels, and responsive smart textiles that alter surface appearance. The intersection of technology and craftsmanship suggests that texture will evolve beyond ornamentation into interactive design. Fringe and textured details represent more than aesthetic trends. They signal a broader sensory renaissance within fashion. In a landscape dominated by flat screens and rapid consumption, texture reintroduces depth, movement, and meaning. It reconnects garments to craftsmanship and invites consumers to engage more fully with what they wear. For designers, incorporating textured elements demands strategic thinking, respect for technique, and clarity of vision. When executed with precision, these fringe benefits transform clothing into experiences—pieces that capture light, encourage motion, and linger in memory. Texture is no longer peripheral to fashion. It is becoming central to how contemporary style is imagined, constructed, and experienced. Texture adds visual depth, movement, and emotional connection, making garments more engaging in both physical and digital spaces. Fringe introduces dynamic movement and versatility, evolving from subcultural roots into refined, luxury fashion applications. Detailed textures signal craftsmanship, time investment, and quality, increasing a garment’s perceived value and desirability. Many techniques like hand embroidery and fabric manipulation support artisans and reduce excess embellishment, aligning with sustainable practices. article_content: The global fashion and textile industry is undergoing a transformation driven by sustainability, efficiency, and innovation. Among the key enablers of this shift is the increasing use of enzymes—biological catalysts that replace harsh chemicals in processes such as desizing, bio-polishing, and denim finishing. While enzymes offer environmental and performance advantages, they also introduce a lesser discussed but critical concern: enzyme dust and occupational exposure risks. As production scales up to meet global demand, the frequency and intensity of worker interaction with enzyme formulations have also increased, elevating potential exposure levels. This makes it essential for manufacturers to balance sustainability goals with robust occupational health safeguards. Greater scrutiny from regulators and sustainability frameworks is further pushing the industry to address these hidden risks more proactively. This article explores the science, risks, real-world implications, and preventive strategies associated with enzyme dust exposure in textile and fashion manufacturing. The Role of Enzymes in Modern Textile Processing Enzymes are protein-based catalysts used to accelerate chemical reactions without being consumed in the process. In textile manufacturing, they are widely applied in: Desizing : Enzymes such as amylases are used to break down starch-based sizing agents applied during weaving. This process ensures efficient removal of residues without damaging the fibres, improving fabric absorbency and preparing it for subsequent wet processing stages. Bio-polishing : Cellulase enzymes are applied to remove microfibrils and surface fuzz from cotton and other cellulosic fabrics. This enhances fabric softness, reduces pilling, and improves colour brightness and sheen, resulting in a higher-quality finish. Denim finishing : Enzymatic treatments, particularly with cellulases, are used as an alternative to traditional stone washing. They help create a worn, faded look while reducing fabric damage, lowering water usage, and minimising the mechanical stress associated with pumice stones. Scouring and bleaching : Enzymes such as pectinases, lipases, and catalases are used to remove natural impurities like waxes, pectins, and residual hydrogen peroxide. This enables cleaner fabric preparation with reduced reliance on harsh alkalis and oxidising agents, leading to lower chemical loads in effluent. Dyeing and colour enhancement : Certain enzymes assist in improving dye uptake and fixation, ensuring more uniform colouration and reducing dye wastage. This contributes to better colour fastness and overall process efficiency. Wastewater treatment and sustainability support : Enzymes are increasingly used in treating textile effluents by breaking down organic pollutants, thereby supporting compliance with environmental regulations and reducing the ecological footprint of textile operations. Their adoption has grown significantly due to their ability to reduce water consumption, lower energy use, and minimise toxic chemical discharge. However, the same biological properties that make enzymes effective also contribute to their potential health risks, especially when they become airborne. These particles are often: Due to their protein-based structure, these particles can trigger biological responses even at very low concentrations once inhaled. The risk is further amplified in poorly ventilated environments where airborne particles can accumulate over time. Additionally, repeated low-level exposure may go unnoticed initially but can lead to sensitisation and more severe health effects with continued contact. Environmental factors such as humidity, airflow patterns, and the method of material handling can further influence how widely these particles disperse within a workspace. Activities like pouring, weighing, or mechanical agitation can significantly increase dust release, intensifying short-term exposure levels. Over time, even intermittent exposure under such conditions can contribute to cumulative health risks for workers. This phenomenon is described as ‘dustiness’, a key determinant of exposure risk alongside enzyme concentration. Occupational Health Risks: What Happens When Workers Are Exposed? 1. Respiratory Sensitisation and Allergies Enzymes are proteins, and when inhaled, they can act as respiratory sensitisers. Repeated exposure may lead to: Studies 1 have shown that enzyme exposure has historically caused respiratory allergy outbreaks, particularly in industrial settings like detergent manufacturing. 2. Long-Term Respiratory Conditions Exposure to airborne particulates in textile environments, including enzyme dust, can contribute to broader respiratory issues. Despite known risks, enzyme dust exposure remains a concern due to several structural and operational challenges: 1. Inconsistent Safety Practices Many textile facilities, especially in developing manufacturing hubs, lack: This leads to uneven implementation of safety measures across the industry. In many cases, safety investments are deprioritised in favour of cost efficiency and production speed, particularly in highly competitive markets. Smaller and medium-scale units may also lack access to advanced technologies or technical expertise required to manage airborne contaminants effectively. 2. Reliance on Powdered Enzymes Powder formulations are still widely used due to: However, they are also the primary source of airborne enzyme dust. Their fine particulate nature makes them highly dispersible during manual handling, increasing the likelihood of inhalation. In facilities where automation is limited, frequent manual dosing and mixing further elevate exposure risks. Despite the availability of safer alternatives, the transition is often slow due to cost constraints and lack of regulatory pressure. 3. Limited Awareness and Training Workers may not be fully aware of: This gap in awareness can result in inconsistent use of protective gear and unsafe handling practices on the shop floor. Training programmes, where they exist, may be infrequent or not sufficiently detailed to address specific risks associated with enzyme exposure. Additionally, language barriers and varying literacy levels in the workforce can further limit the effectiveness of safety communication and compliance. Industry Response: Moving Towards Safer Alternatives Recognising the risks, industry organisations and certification systems are increasingly promoting safer practices. 1. Shift to Liquid and Encapsulated Enzymes Liquid formulations and coated granules: Some certification systems have gone further by restricting the use of powder enzymes altogether in approved textile production. 2. Adoption of the ‘Hierarchy of Controls’ Effective risk management follows a structured approach: This multi-layered strategy is essential for reducing exposure risk. Implications for the Fashion Industry The issue of enzyme dust intersects with broader themes in fashion: 1. Ethical Manufacturing Worker safety is increasingly tied to brand accountability. Consumers and stakeholders are demanding: Brands are now expected to go beyond compliance and actively ensure that their sourcing practices do not compromise worker health at any stage of production. Increased public scrutiny, driven by media and advocacy groups, has made occupational safety a visible component of corporate social responsibility. 2. Sustainability vs. Safety Trade-Off While enzymes are promoted as eco-friendly alternatives, their use must be balanced with occupational health considerations. This highlights a critical need to adopt a more holistic definition of sustainability, one that equally prioritises environmental impact and human well-being. Therefore, integrating health impact evaluations into sustainability strategies is essential to avoid shifting risks from the environment to workers. 3. Regulatory and Certification Pressure Frameworks such as sustainable textile certifications are pushing manufacturers to: Compliance with these frameworks is increasingly becoming a prerequisite for market access, particularly in international supply chains. Certifications not only drive safer practices but also encourage continuous improvement through regular audits and performance benchmarks. As regulations tighten, companies that proactively adopt higher safety standards are likely to gain a competitive advantage and strengthen their position in the global market. The Way Forward Addressing enzyme dust exposure requires coordinated action across the value chain: In addition, industry-wide collaboration and knowledge-sharing platforms can play a crucial role in standardising best practices and accelerating the adoption of safer technologies. Investment in research and innovation will further help develop enzyme solutions that are both high-performing and inherently low-risk. Continuous monitoring, reporting, and improvement should be embedded into operational frameworks to ensure long-term worker safety. Ultimately, the goal is to ensure that sustainability innovations do not come at the cost of worker health. Enzymes have revolutionised textile processing, offering a pathway towards cleaner and more efficient fashion production. However, the emergence of enzyme dust as an occupational hazard highlights a critical gap in the industry’s sustainability narrative The science is clear: airborne enzyme exposure can pose serious respiratory risks if not properly managed. The solutions are equally clear: safer formulations, better engineering controls, and systemic risk management. As the fashion industry continues to evolve, integrating worker safety into sustainability frameworks will be essential. Only then can the industry truly claim to be both environmentally and socially responsible. article_content: The global textile and clothing industry is undergoing a significant structural shift. For decades, China has been the world’s largest apparel producer, supported by its vast manufacturing base, integrated supply chains, and advanced technologies. In recent years, however, rising production costs, evolving trade dynamics, and geopolitical uncertainty have compelled international companies to rethink their sourcing strategies. As a result, countries such as Bangladesh and Vietnam are gaining prominence in the evolving global textile landscape. From Cost Advantage to Strategic Shift: Bangladesh’s Rising Role Bangladesh has emerged as a major clothing exporter, driven by its low labour costs, extensive manufacturing capacity, and preferential access to key markets, particularly in Europe. Over the past decade, the country has also strengthened its position as a reliable sourcing destination, supported by stricter compliance standards and improved worker safety in manufacturing. As brands diversify away from concentrated production hubs, these gains have enabled Bangladesh to capture a growing share of global apparel orders. However, the redistribution of global textile orders is neither linear nor without risk. Heightened scrutiny of supply chains, particularly in certain industrial regions, has prompted buyers to adopt more diversified sourcing strategies, shifting parts of production and logistics across multiple countries. This rise of indirect and multi-country supply chains is increasing demand across several Asian manufacturing hubs. While such shifts may create new opportunities, they are also intensifying regional competition and could lead to fluctuations in order volumes for established exporters like Bangladesh. Vietnam’s rapid advancement underscores the need to integrate technology into global sourcing strategies. The country has invested heavily in advanced textiles, automation, and digital production techniques. These investments have transformed Vietnam into a modern manufacturing hub, effectively balancing efficiency with sustainability. At the same time, India is working to strengthen its global position, leveraging its abundant raw materials and supportive policies for technical textiles. These developments reflect a broader shift in the textile sector, moving from a singular focus on cost reduction towards a model centred on value-added, technology-driven production. Balancing Growth Pressures with Future-Ready Transformation In the coming years, however, Bangladesh’s long-standing advantage, built on affordable labour, may come under pressure. Rising living costs and greater recognition of workers’ rights are likely to influence future wage negotiations. While improvements in pay and working conditions are essential for social stability, abrupt increases without corresponding productivity gains could strain already vulnerable businesses. Balancing economic competitiveness with equitable progress is therefore becoming increasingly critical. The global textile trade is shaped not only by internal dynamics but also by external pressures. Fluctuations in energy costs, disruptions to key shipping routes, and new environmental regulations in major consumer markets are reshaping production and distribution patterns. These uncertainties heighten the need for export-dependent nations to build resilience through market diversification, stronger industrial capabilities, and closer collaboration between policymakers, industry leaders, and research institutions. Today, Bangladesh’s textile industry stands at a critical juncture. The sector must reduce its reliance on labour-intensive models and transition towards modern machinery, automation, and workforce upskilling to remain competitive in global supply chains. By investing in technical textiles, sustainable manufacturing practices, and innovation-led production, the country can move up the value chain and become less vulnerable to cost fluctuations. The global textile industry is undergoing a clear transformation. Bangladesh has so far prospered due to its scale and competitive edge, but its future growth will depend on how effectively it adapts to evolving technologies, regulations, and global dynamics. With decisive policy action and strategic investment, the country can sustain its position as a leading apparel exporter while building a more resilient and diversified textile sector. Bangladesh’s textile industry is no longer competing on cost alone but at a crossroads where resilience, innovation, and value creation will define its future. As global supply chains become more fragmented and competitive, the country must accelerate its transition towards technology-driven manufacturing, sustainable practices, and skilled labour development. Strategic alignment between industry and policy will be essential to manage cost pressures while enhancing productivity. If navigated effectively, Bangladesh can not only retain its position in global apparel trade but also evolve into a more diversified, future-ready textile powerhouse. Rising wages, increasing competition from countries like Vietnam and India, and shifts towards multi-country supply chains may lead to fluctuating order volumes and margin pressures. By investing in automation, sustainable practices, technical textiles, and workforce upskilling, Bangladesh can move up the value chain and strengthen long-term competitiveness. article_title: Khes Weaving: Textiles from the Punjab Plains
sub_title: Khes is a handwoven cotton textile from Punjab, traditionally used as a blanket, bedspread, shawl, or floor covering. It was an essential household item, valued for its durability, warmth, and versatility in daily and ceremonial use. Khes is distinguished by its bold geometric patterns, use of simple weave structures like plain and twill, and techniques such as double-cloth weaving, which create reversible fabrics with intricate designs. Khes is primarily made from cotton yarn, often hand-spun.
article_content: Across the rural landscapes of Punjab, textiles have historically played a vital role in everyday life and domestic culture. Among the region’s traditional fabrics, khes stands out as a humble yet culturally significant handwoven textile that was once an essential component of Punjabi households. Characterised by bold checks, stripes, and geometric patterns, khes served not only as a utilitarian fabric but also as a symbol of warmth, craftsmanship, and community identity. Although the craft now survives only in limited pockets, its history reflects a deep connection between people, place, and textile traditions. Origins and Historical Background Khes weaving originated in the Punjab region of the Indian subcontinent, historically encompassing areas that now fall within both India and Pakistan. While the craft gained prominence during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the broader tradition of cotton weaving in the region dates back much earlier, particularly to the Mughal period when textile production flourished under royal patronage. Traditionally, khes was woven as a thin cotton blanket or covering intended for everyday domestic use. Its versatility allowed it to function as a bedspread, shawl, wrap, or floor covering during gatherings and ceremonies. In rural households, khes was often woven by women using simple pit looms installed within the home. Consequently, the making of khes became closely associated with domestic craftsmanship and familial care. In many Punjabi communities, khes also carried emotional and cultural significance. Mothers and grandmothers frequently wove khes pieces for daughters as part of their dowry, symbolising protection, warmth, and continuity of tradition. Over time, particular patterns and colour combinations came to represent regional identities and local preferences. Textile Structure and Weaving Types The structure of khes is defined by relatively simple yet effective weaving techniques that produce a durable and breathable fabric. The most common weave structures include plain weave and twill weave. In a plain weave, warp and weft threads intersect alternately, producing a balanced and strong fabric structure. This technique creates the characteristic grid-like patterns seen in many khes textiles, where bold checks and stripes emerge through the use of alternating coloured yarns. In certain regions, particularly in western Punjab (now part of Pakistan), weavers historically practiced double cloth weaving, a more complex technique in which two layers of fabric are woven simultaneously and interchanged to form intricate patterns. Double-cloth khes often displayed more elaborate motifs and were reversible, making them highly valued. The weaving process was traditionally carried out on pit looms, locally known as ‘khaddi’. These looms are partially installed below ground level, allowing the weaver to maintain better tension and control while producing sturdy cotton textiles. Due to the limited width of traditional looms, khes was typically woven in two narrow panels, which were later stitched together along the centre seam to form a wider textile. Materials and Dyeing Practices Cotton yarn is the primary material used in khes weaving. Historically, coarse hand-spun cotton was commonly used, giving the fabric its characteristic texture and weight. In certain cases, finer cotton or cotton–silk blends were incorporated, particularly for ceremonial or special purpose pieces. Traditional khes textiles relied heavily on natural dyes derived from plant and mineral sources. Indigo produced deep blue shades, madder root generated rich red tones, turmeric provided yellow hues, and ferrous oxide produced darker shades. These colours were often combined to create striking contrasts in the woven patterns. Because the design of khes emerges from the interlacing of coloured yarns, the dyeing and preparation of yarns play a critical role in the final textile. Warp threads are carefully arranged according to the intended pattern so that stripes and checks align precisely once the fabric is woven. Motifs, Designs, and Patterns Historically, khes textiles could be easily identified by their provenance, lineage, and status through variations in weave structures, patterns, colour combinations, and yarn quality. Khes originating from western Punjab, particularly from regions such as Sindh, Sargodha, and Multan, were distinguished by vibrant colours and complex patterns. These textiles typically featured smaller all-over motifs in the body, complemented by bold geometric borders forming a char bagh layout at the four corners. Such textiles were known as Majnoo Khes, sometimes referred to as Laila-Majnoo Khes or Sindhi Khes. Majnoo khes were thicker and heavier due to the double-cloth weaving technique. The additional threads often created contrasting colour compositions on either side, making the fabric reversible. These textiles typically ended with tightly woven bands and finely hand-rolled tassels. Another variation was Gumti Khes, characterised by smaller repetitive motifs across the body and simple borders. The motifs, often called buto in the Sindh region, were created using the dobby weaving technique. Unlike Majnoo khes, Gumti khes were lighter and more flexible, making them suitable for use as shawls or coverlets. Several patterns carried distinctive regional names, including: Simpler textiles known as Saada Khes were woven in plain, twill, or herringbone weaves. These textiles often featured striped or checkered patterns and were lighter compared to the dense double-woven khes. Saada khes frequently displayed a distinctive cord like detail a few inches inward from the selvage before the tassels began. Processes, Tools, and Techniques The production of khes involves several stages, each requiring skill and careful attention. The process begins with raw cotton procurement and spinning. Cotton, locally known as ‘soot’, was spun into coarse yarn using hand spindles or the ambar charkha. The resulting yarn typically ranged between 20s and 30s counts and often displayed a slightly slubbed texture. The spun yarn was preserved in large skeins and taken to local dyers, known as ‘rangrez’, who washed the yarn to prevent shrinkage and dyed it using natural pigments. After dyeing, the yarn was wound onto spools for warping. The weaving process was carried out on pit looms, which were installed over pits approximately 24 to 28 inches deep. The pit helped maintain moisture levels and improved weaving conditions. Both men and women participated in the weaving process, although many oral accounts suggest that women traditionally played a major role. Patterns in khes were largely weft driven, meaning the motifs emerged through careful manipulation of the weft threads. The threads were compacted using a comb like tool known as ‘hatthi’ or ‘kanghi’, which ensured tight and even weaving. By the late 1960s, many khes weaving centres transitioned to power looms, although some smaller centres and individual artisans continued producing handwoven khes for commissioned orders. Cultural Meaning and Social Role Beyond its technical characteristics, khes occupies an important place in the social and cultural life of Punjab. In rural households, it served as a versatile textile used for bedding, shawls, wraps, and floor coverings during gatherings. For elderly women, khes often functioned as a shawl-like wrap, providing warmth and modesty. Because many khes were woven within the household, the textile carried a strong emotional connection between the maker and the user. The association of khes with dowry traditions further strengthened its cultural significance. A khes woven by a mother or grandmother symbolised care, continuity, and blessings for a daughter beginning a new life in another household. Partition and Transformation of the Craft The Partition of India in 1947 had a profound impact on khes weaving. Before the political division, khes production extended across the entire Punjab region, facilitating exchange of techniques and cultural influences. Western Punjab, which became part of Pakistan, had a strong tradition of double-cloth khes weaving with complex patterns. Eastern Punjab in India primarily produced simpler striped and checked khes. Partition disrupted these networks of artisans and knowledge exchange, resulting in the gradual disappearance of certain weaving traditions, particularly the double-cloth technique on the Indian side. Present Day Challenges Today, khes weaving faces several challenges that threaten its survival as a living craft tradition. One major challenge is competition from machine-made textiles, which are widely available at lower prices. Additionally, the number of skilled artisans has declined significantly, as younger generations often seek alternative occupations offering greater economic stability. In areas where khes is still produced, weavers frequently work with standardised designs intended for low-cost markets. This has led to a decline in both the diversity of patterns and the quality of the fabric. Furthermore, the disappearance of traditional knowledge systems has resulted in the loss of complex techniques such as double-cloth weaving. Efforts Towards Revival Despite these challenges, khes has recently begun to attract renewed attention among designers, researchers, and craft organisations. Vintage khes textiles are increasingly valued for their distinctive aesthetics, durability, and cultural heritage. Contemporary designers are experimenting with khes patterns and structures to develop products such as scarves, stoles, upholstery fabrics, and home décor textiles. These adaptations aim to create new market opportunities while preserving the visual identity of the traditional fabric. Such initiatives also align with the growing global interest in sustainable and handmade textiles. Handloom fabrics like khes require minimal energy and rely largely on natural materials, making them environmentally responsible alternatives to industrial textile production. Khes weaving represents a rich textile heritage shaped by generations of artisans across the Punjab region. From its origins as a household craft to its role in cultural rituals and daily life, khes reflects the deep relationship between textiles and community identity. Although the craft faces numerous challenges today, renewed interest in handloom traditions offers hope for its revival. By documenting its history, preserving its techniques, and exploring new possibilities for its application, khes can continue to remain a meaningful part of the textile landscape of the Indian subcontinent. Khes is a handwoven cotton textile from Punjab, traditionally used as a blanket, bedspread, shawl, or floor covering. It was an essential household item, valued for its durability, warmth, and versatility in daily and ceremonial use. Khes is distinguished by its bold geometric patterns, use of simple weave structures like plain and twill, and techniques such as double-cloth weaving, which create reversible fabrics with intricate designs. Khes is primarily made from cotton yarn, often hand-spun. Traditionally, natural dyes such as indigo, madder, turmeric, and iron-based compounds were used to create vibrant and contrasting colours. The craft faces decline due to competition from cheaper machine-made textiles, reduced artisan participation, loss of traditional knowledge, and limited market demand for high-quality handmade khes. The capsule wardrobe may no longer have a precise definition, but it's changing the way consumers think about their clothing. A consciously curated wardrobe with a few, high-quality pieces creates a sustainable solution to the pollution problems posted by fast-fashion. Younger fashion-forward buyers are latching onto the capsule wardrobe movement, and thus disrupting the clothing industry. Here's the past, present, and future of the capsule wardrobe, and a few specific pieces that many consumers are looking for to complete their minimalist look. The Origins of the Capsule Wardrobe Susie Faux, owner of the London-based boutique Wardrobe first coined the term "capsule wardrobe" as early as the 1970s. Faux described a capsule wardrobe as a small collection of essential clothing items that never go out of style. The original capsule wardrobe included skirts, pants, tops, and coats with a few seasonable items peppered throughout. The idea was golden from the onset, but Donna Karan made the concept even more popular in 1985, when she released her own line of seven interchangeable professional pieces. These "7 Easy Pieces" of clothing, as we would now describe them, went viral. The popularity of the capsule wardrobe continued to grow over the years, specifically in Britain and America. It is now a common term referring to a small collection of interchangeable clothing , allowing the wearer to create a large number of outfits from a few coordinating items. The key to the capsule wardrobe remains a combination of classic styles and neutral colors. The Official Guidelines to Creating the Capsule There are five basic rules to follow when creating a capsule wardrobe. When consumers abide by these simple considerations, they are able to easily generate a long-lasting, coordinating capsule that fits the bill. 1. Body Shape. When buyers know what cuts and styles look best on their body, they are able to maximize these looks, and avoid all other, non-ideal clothing cuts. Every piece of the capsule wardrobe should be flattering to the owner's unique body composition. 2.   Skin Tone. Similarly to the body shape consideration, buyers should pay attention to colors that aid the wearer in a               healthy, bright appearance. Skin tone is one of the key considerations when following the next guideline… 3.   Color Scheme. A capsule wardrobe typically consists of two to three colors that mesh well with each other (and basically everything else.) Popular colors include the classic black, white and grey, as well as brown and navy blue. Every piece, including accessories like coats and handbags, should abide by the color scheme. A few scarves and accessories may give a pop of bolder colour, but that depends on the style of the wearer. 4.   Shapes and Patterns. Some patterns are part of fleeting fads, and may show their age more quickly than others. Those looking to create a truly timeless capsule wardrobe should turn to classic patterns, like stripes and solids. 5.   Quality. Last, but certainly not least, owners of capsule wardrobes must seek out individual items that will last for a long time. High-quality clothing will allow for daily wear, and also more versatility in how clothing is used. The Basic Staples of a Capsule Wardrobe A sample capsule wardrobe can include anywhere from 10 to 40 items, but the bare-bones basics are listed below with some classic sample pieces. Trench Coat This trench coat from ASOS is versatile and neutral, with the ability to be dressed up or down. Skinny Jeans Everlane is a great source for classic, high-quality skinny jeans like these. White Shirt Every capsule wardrobe needs a timeless white shirt, like this piece by Calvin Klein. LBD (Little Black Dress) When it comes to the LBD, buyers need not look further than The Devlin Dress by M.M. Lafleur. In addition to these classic pieces, a capsule wardrobe will also require various t-shirts and camisole tops, a sweater or two, a pair of boots (like these from Madewell), flats and heels, and a few bags or purses for everyday wear. Simplicity and Sustainability The capsule wardrobe shows a clear movement toward a more sustainable fashion system . When consumers buy less, and keep their clothing for a longer period of time, there is a bit of relief in the pounds of clothing being sent to landfills. The simplicity of the capsule wardrobe is also an advantage for buyers who want to stress less about their clothing choices. This simple, sustainable change in closets across the globe mirrors a more eco-conscious consumer base when it comes to everyday fashion. article_title: The True Textile Revolution: Delivering a Circular, Responsible, Accessible and Desirable Fashion Industry
sub_title: The fashion industry is criticised for its heavy use of natural resources, reliance on fossil fuels, polluting dyeing processes and the generation of large volumes of textile waste. The rise of fast and ultra-fast fashion has accelerated production and consumption cycles, intensifying environmental pressure and contributing to resource depletion and pollution across the supply chain.
