article_title: Community Brands: Weaving Fashion and People Together
sub_title: A community brand is a label built around the values, needs, and identity of a specific group, where the brand exists to serve and connect people rather than just sell products. They foster authentic connections, build trust, and create loyal customer bases by aligning with shared values, offering experiences, and encouraging participation. By cultivating real connections, hosting events, engaging on digital platforms, encouraging user content, aligning with meaningful causes, and maintaining au
article_content: In today’s fashion industry, success is not just about selling garments. It is about building a community. The term ‘community brand’ has become a buzzword in textile and apparel circles, reflecting a shift in how brands engage with consumers. From global sportswear giants hosting local meetups to indie designers co-creating with fans, community-driven brands are reshaping how people experience fashion. This article explores what community brands are in the context of apparel and textiles, why they matter, and how they are transforming the industry through authentic connections. What Are Community Brands in Fashion? Community brands are labels that place a community of people at the heart of their identity and strategy. Traditionally, marketers spoke of brand communities—groups of fans emotionally attached to a brand or product. These are the Harley-Davidson rider clubs or sneakerhead forums united by love for a label. Such brand communities “connect customers with like-minded influencers and peers, becoming trusted sources of information and supportive spaces” 1 for sharing experiences. In fashion, think of the cult followings behind streetwear drops or luxury house fan clubs. A community brand, however, flips that concept: rather than a community forming around a brand, the brand itself is formed in service to a community 2 . In other words, the brand exists to champion the needs, values, or identity of a group of people. This could be a social or cultural community (e.g. outdoor enthusiasts, plus-size women, sustainability advocates) or a lifestyle movement. The apparel sector offers plenty of examples—from a yoga-wear label built around a wellness community to a streetwear collective born from skate culture. In both cases, the clothing is almost secondary to the sense of belonging and purpose the brand cultivates. A community brand “is not just an activewear brand—it is a community, a lifestyle, and a movement,” as one analysis of Lululemon’s success puts it. Why Fashion Brands Are Embracing Community? Several trends are pushing fashion and textile companies towards community-centric branding. Consumer trust and attention have become harder to earn in the digital age. Traditional celebrity endorsements and influencer marketing are losing their edge as audiences grow weary of incessant sponsored content. In fact, the influencer landscape has become so crowded that authenticity can suffer. Many consumers now suspect influencers “prioritise payday over genuine product passion,” leading to waning trust. Facing this ‘influencer fatigue’, brands see community-building as a more genuine way to connect. Recommendations from real peers or fellow enthusiasts carry more credibility than paid posts. As marketing experts observe, community-based marketing leverages the collective voice of a brand’s own customers instead of big-name influencers, fostering organic advocacy rooted in real passion 3 . At the same time, the rise of social media and digital platforms has made it easier for like-minded people to find each other—and for brands to engage them directly. Fashion shoppers today do not just buy products; they join tribes. Whether it is sneakerheads on Discord, cottagecore aficionados on Instagram, or ethical fashion supporters on Reddit, micro-communities drive trends and loyalty. A 2024 industry report by Forbes highlighted that fashion brand communities have become “trusted spaces” that incubate trends and loyal consumer bases in this era of hyper-connected niches. In short, modern consumers—especially Gen Z and millennials—crave belonging and alignment of values. They gravitate towards brands that stand for something and bring people together—be it a cause, a sport, or a lifestyle. An Edelman survey found 84 per cent of consumers globally say they need to share values with a brand before they will support it—a telling statistic behind the community brand movement 4 . Finally, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the community trend. With physical interactions limited, many brands turned to online communities, virtual events, and grassroots engagement to maintain loyalty. This proved the power of community even when stores were closed. Post-pandemic, those community bonds remain a strategic asset as companies rebuild and innovate. Benefits of Building a Community Brand Shifting from a product-centric to a community-centric approach offers numerous benefits for fashion and textile businesses: For consumers, being part of a brand community enhances their experience too. They get a supportive network, exclusive perks or knowledge, and a sense of identity through the brand. In essence, a community brand weaves value beyond the product, creating a lifestyle ecosystem that customers love to be part of. How to Build a Community-Centric Fashion Brand? Fostering a genuine community around a fashion label requires strategic effort and authenticity. Brands leading the way provide a playbook of tactics: Challenges and Keys to Success While the community brand model is powerful, it is not a magic wand. Brands venturing into community-building should be mindful of several challenges: Despite these challenges, the trend is clear: community-building in fashion is shifting from a ‘nice-to-have’ to a ‘must-have’ in the industry playbook. As one analysis noted, a community-driven brand was once a novelty, but is increasingly seen as an essential strategy in modern fashion, provided the brand has a solid foundation to build on. The brands that succeed are those who genuinely value their community and see customers not just as buyers, but as active participants in the brand’s story. The emergence of community brands in the textile and apparel industry marks a return to what fashion has always been about at its core: human connection. Clothing has the power to bring people together—whether through shared interests, common values, or collective creativity—and forward-thinking brands are leveraging that power. By cultivating communities, fashion labels large and small are achieving more sustainable success: loyal customers, authentic advocacy, and a cultural relevance that no advertisement budget can buy. In a world saturated with choices, community brands offer something deeper than a product. They offer belonging—to a tribe, a mission, a lifestyle. As we move further towards 2030, expect more brands to weave community into the very fabric of their identity. The future of fashion will be written not just by designers or marketers, but by communities of passionate individuals rallying around brands that speak to them and with them. And that truly is a beautiful fit. A community brand is a label built around the values, needs, and identity of a specific group, where the brand exists to serve and connect people rather than just sell products. They foster authentic connections, build trust, and create loyal customer bases by aligning with shared values, offering experiences, and encouraging participation. By cultivating real connections, hosting events, engaging on digital platforms, encouraging user content, aligning with meaningful causes, and maintaining authentic communication. Key challenges include ensuring authenticity, balancing customer input with brand identity, dedicating sufficient resources, and managing criticism or conflicts effectively. article_title: Transforming Apparel and Textile Operations through ERP Systems
sub_title: ERP systems are vital in this industry due to its highly dynamic nature. They streamline operations, reduce data redundancy, and improve coordination across departments, ensuring efficient order processing, production planning, and inventory management. An ERP system integrates key functions such as sales, procurement, inventory control, production, quality control, dispatch, finance, and HR. It provides real-time access to data across departments, facilitating better decision-making and respons
article_content: The textile and apparel industry are undergoing constant transformation driven by rapidly evolving fashion trends. These dynamic trends foster the development of new styles and textile innovations, necessitating continuous gatekeeping and timely interventions. Unlike the automotive industry—where a single vehicle model can remain in production for years with minimal variation—the garment and textile sector witnesses continuous and minute-to-minute fluctuations. In such a volatile environment, Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems play a critical role in enhancing efficiency and eliminating data redundancy in organisations. ERP is a comprehensive business management tool that integrates various departmental functions and transactions within an organisation. It enables seamless interdepartmental communication and real-time data access, enhancing operational efficiency and responsiveness ( Kamal, Mostafa, 2018) . ERP systems became essential as the industry sought to minimise data redundancy and operate with greater intelligence and efficiency. ERP is a unified software solution that captures and records the activities of all departments within an organisation. It comprises various modules that correspond to key departmental functions such as sales, procurement, inventory management, and order planning. Prior to the advent of ERP, these functions were managed through isolated systems, often resulting in data silos and inefficiencies. The integration provided by ERP has consolidated these formerly disparate systems into a cohesive platform, significantly streamlining operations and decision-making processes (Hui et.al, 2010) Working of ERP Software in the apparel industry To understand how ERP software functions, consider an example from the garment industry. When the merchandising team receives new shirt orders, they enter them directly into the ERP system. The planning department can then access the same order to organise the distribution of materials, labour, and machinery accordingly. Simultaneously, the procurement team reviews the production order, checks for material availability within the retail inventory, and, if needed, places a vendor order—all through the ERP system. Once the materials arrive, the inventory department records their receipt in the ERP software. The production team then raises a material request, and the store department issues the required items using a store indent generated via the system. Manufacturing details such as machine allocation, operator name, and order number are also recorded within the ERP platform. After production, the finished goods go through a quality control (QC) process, and the results are updated in the system. The dispatch team then uses the ERP software to generate a packing list and dispatch order. The products are packaged as per the packing list, and an invoice is automatically created by the ERP system. Subsequently, a delivery challan and gate pass are generated through the software. When payment is received, the funds are recorded in the accounts receivable module of the ERP system, closing the transaction loop. This example highlights the critical role of ERP software in streamlining operations across departments and ensuring seamless coordination throughout the supply chain in the garment industry. Different ERP software used by the apparel and textile industry ERP software captures and records every activity within an apparel company, enabling all departments to monitor order statuses in real time. This fosters a well-coordinated operational structure, reducing the risk of errors and ensuring smoother workflow management. As competition intensifies and profit margins shrink, stakeholders in the apparel and textile industries increasingly recognise the importance of cost control and optimal utilisation of enterprise resources. ERP systems directly address these challenges by streamlining processes, enhancing efficiency, and supporting strategic decision-making. By automating routine tasks, ERP software not only helps lower operational costs but also improves employee satisfaction through seamless interdepartmental communication. Its advanced, customisable features allow businesses to tailor solutions to their specific needs, capturing both tangible cost savings and intangible benefits such as improved responsiveness and agility (Ranjan, Jha & Pal, 2016). Several ERP software solutions are currently available in the market, offering diverse functionalities to suit varying business requirements are discussed below: Software Function FDM4 It is developed to meet the rapidly changing demands of the apparel industry and designed to ensure communication across systems from ASNs to shipping labels. It also includes EDI capabilities, inventory and purchasing applications, integrated accounting, and advanced business analytics. It offers complete resource management services that are tailored to the demands of the fashion sector. The system can be customised on an individual basis and covers every step of the fashion business, from product distribution and design to manufacturing, private brand wholesale, and retail. The portal is specifically created by apparel producers to directly assist international buying houses. Due to its highly specific toolkit, which includes product development, marking and cut processing, order management, WIP processing, demand-based bill-of-materials processing, inventory control, purchasing, BI reporting, production planning, carton packing, CMT & outsourcing operations, task management processing, AQL, and QC, the system enables the apparel enterprise to run smoothly. It has been a top fashion solution on the market for more than 25 years. PLM processing, sophisticated warehouse management features, order processing, financial reporting, and inventory management are all included in one completely integrated system, additionally to separate telemarketing and catalogue components. Along with being efficient at mobility, the system has the special capacity to create and distribute social network messages that are generated inside. This system, which was created especially for the clothing sector, provides an integrated ERP and product lifecycle management (PLM) capacity. This extensive platform offers value across multiple domains, including style development, product execution, and worldwide buyer distribution. Along with the more common manufacturing procedures like BOM and PSV, it also has capabilities like cut planning, fabric inspection, CMT production, and two-dimensional size ranging. Additionally, it has a thorough order auditing capacity. It is designed for fashion and apparel businesses, which offers real-time insights and industry-specific functionality. RDPL It offers tailored solutions for the fashion industry, ensuring seamless integration, enhanced ROI and robust online presence through mobile and website development. NOW ERP from Datatex It is notable for its adaptability to a wide range of business procedures and its capacity to meet the requirements of the industry, such as handling a wide variety of products. Using object-oriented technology, the program facilitates the traceability and dynamic integration of business activities from the fibre stage to the finished product. For Industry 4.0 breakthroughs, it incorporates cutting-edge web technologies like Jakarta EE, web services, and XML. WFX It has a modern and latest technology interface which is user-friendly and easy to use. All manufacturing processes, including costing, sampling, budgeting, supplier cooperation, buying, material planning, quality control, order administration, and so forth, can be tracked and digitalised with its assistance. Datatex ERP is widely adopted by major Indian textile and apparel companies such as Arvind, ABRFL, Vardhman, and the Bhilwara Group. Initially implemented on the AS400 platform, Datatex transitioned to a web-based system in 2004, significantly expanding its global reach. Designed to cater to small, medium, and large enterprises, Datatex offers scalable solutions across the textile value chain. Another prominent player, World Fashion Exchange (WFX) , was established in 2000. It began with an EDP/EDI solution tailored for brands and fashion agents in India. Over time, WFX evolved into a comprehensive ERP system. A notable example of successful implementation is Gokaldas Exports , which has leveraged WFX to streamline operations. Export houses like Ranger and Laguna have also reported enhanced production efficiency and seamless workflows following ERP integration ( Mindya & Wickramasinghe , 2012). Advantages of Using ERP in the Apparel and Textile Industry Implementing an agile ERP system in the textile and apparel sector can significantly streamline operations and reduce costs. When processes are well-organised, companies can cut operational and administrative expenses by up to 15 per cent , thanks to fewer manual errors, improved time management, and increased employee satisfaction. Below are the key advantages of ERP implementation in the textile and garment industry: 1. ERP provides a unified dashboard that integrates multiple departments— Quality Control, Production, Supply Chain Planning, RCCP, Warehouse Management, Finance, HR, Sales, Marketing, and Shop Floor Operations —enabling seamless coordination and control. 2. ERP systems deliver accurate and reliable, real-time data to authorised users, allowing remote access from anywhere in the world. This improves decision-making speed, boosts productivity, and enhances collaboration with suppliers, customers, and internal teams. 3. ERP ensures the optimal mix of inventory across the organisation. Its agile and mobile warehouse management features help avoid excess inventory or shortages, promoting a systematic and cost-efficient supply chain. 4. ERP systems enable better task assignment by matching the most suitable employee to specific jobs, ensuring timely completion of purchase orders. Additionally, they minimise errors, eliminate redundant data entry, and reduce other repetitive administrative tasks thereby improving efficiency and proper time management. 5. The traditional manual methods of tracking replenishment or stock transfers are replaced by ERP’s real-time monitoring capabilities. It enables live tracking and reporting across the shop floor, warehouse, procurement, and logistics , enhancing responsiveness and operational efficiency. Job Titles Associated with ERP The field of ERP encompasses several job titles that often overlap, and each ERP system may have unique variations of these roles. This can make it challenging to navigate the different responsibilities and functions tied to ERP systems. However, here are some core ERP job titles: 1. There are ERP Specialists who focus on maintaining, customising, and optimising ERP software to ensure smooth operations across an organisation. 2. The Support Staff provide ongoing technical support to end-users, resolving issues related to ERP systems. 3. The ERP Consultants advise organisations on the best ERP solutions based on their needs, and assist with the implementation, integration, and customisation of ERP systems. 4. The ERP Business Analysts analyse business requirements and workflows to identify the most suitable ERP solutions. They ensure that the ERP system aligns with business processes. 5. The ERP Software Developers customise and develop ERP systems by writing code, building modules, and integrating different functions to ensure the system meets the organisation’s needs. 6. A business may also hire ERP Project Managers who oversee the implementation and deployment of ERP systems, manage resources, timelines, and ensure that projects meet business objectives. To succeed in these roles, professionals need a blend of technical and business-oriented skills, including technical proficiency like knowledge of database management, data analysis tools, and programming languages; greater analytical abilities to assess business processes and find solutions that improve efficiency; project management skills of planning, organising, and coordinating ERP implementation and updates; problem-solving skills, and the ability to clearly communicate with both technical teams and business stakeholders; and accuracy in managing complex ERP systems and understanding of how ERP integrates with overall business operations. As the field is dynamic in nature, individuals must also stay adaptable to new software developments and tools. ERP systems play a critical role in managing textile operations across all stages—from planning and development to manufacturing and distribution. The textile industry is shifting from isolated, custom programming to integrated ERP systems, which streamline operations and enhance efficiency. Many textile mills are adopting ERP and web-based solutions to stay competitive in an ever-evolving industry. ERP systems help track raw materials, monitor inventory, and maintain comprehensive records, enabling better decision-making and resource management. These systems are increasingly essential for both small and large enterprises, offering customisation to meet specific business needs. The fast-paced changes in the fashion and apparel sectors are compelling companies, especially in developing economies, to implement ERP systems. article_content: In the apparel industry, pattern engineering and drafting are crucial processes that determine garment quality and fit. Traditionally, these tasks were performed manually, relying heavily on skilled labour without automation or technology. Even today, some small-scale industries continue to use manual pattern-making techniques. However, as technology advances, the adoption of software for pattern-making has become essential to meet modern business demands. Manual pattern-making is becoming increasingly impractical due to the need for shorter order delivery lead times, larger business volumes, and the efficiency demands of today’s market. The advent of artificial intelligence and advanced technology has revolutionised pattern-making and design, making these processes faster and more efficient. These technologies reduce lead time, minimise fabric wastage, and shorten the time required for drafting and cutting. Additionally, they lower the need for excess manpower, reduce manufacturing costs, and improve marker efficiency and cutting quality, while offering greater flexibility to meet customer requirements. Pattern-making software falls under the category of computer-aided design (CAD) systems, which are primarily used for designing, pattern-making, and pattern grading. Before delving into specific software, it is essential to understand the fundamentals of pattern-making. Pattern-making involves transforming a sketch into a digital image, which is then printed on a marker. The placement and nesting of these designed patterns determine the overall marker efficiency. Maximising fabric utilisation results in higher marker efficiency, contributing to cost-effective production. In the fast-evolving world of fashion, pattern-making software plays a crucial role in enhancing the manufacturing process by converting creative designs into garment production. Advancements in cutting, sewing, and pattern engineering offer various solutions that improve the quality and efficiency of apparel production. Today, there are numerous software options available, ranging from budget-friendly tools to high-end professional suites. The right choice of software depends on its intended application and specific needs. Some popular pattern-making software in the apparel industry include Clo 3D, Browzwear, StyleCAD, Audaces, Assyst Bullmer, EFI Optitex, Lectra Modaris, Polygonal Design PatternMaker, Lectra, Optitex, Tuka CAD, Gerber Accumark, Richpeace, Crea, GT CAD Software, Etelestia, Fashion CAD, Gemini CAD System, PAD System, Romans CAD, Dimension CAD, Wild Ginger, and Tukatech. These tools offer a range of features, from 2D and 3D pattern design to digital fabric simulation, allowing designers to create, modify, and perfect garment patterns with precision and efficiency. The Evolution of Pattern-Making Manual Pattern Making : Pattern-making initially began as a manual process using paper, pencils, rulers, and scissors. It was labour-intensive and relied heavily on the skill of the pattern maker, making it prone to errors. Introduction of CAD (Computer-Aided Design) Systems : In the late 20th century, CAD systems were introduced, allowing designers to create digital patterns. This transition reduced manual drafting time while improving accuracy and efficiency. Integration of CAD with CAM Systems : The integration of CAD with computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) systems enabled automated cutting and sewing processes. This seamless transition from design to production streamlined workflows and reduced lead times. 3D Pattern Making and Virtual Prototyping : In the early 21st century, 3D pattern making emerged, allowing designers to visualise garments in a 3D environment. This technology reduced the need for physical prototypes, saving both time and resources. Cloud-Based and Collaborative Platforms : Cloud-based solutions enabled real-time collaboration among designers, pattern makers, and manufacturers. These platforms improved communication, version control, and project management across different locations. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning : AI and machine learning have transformed pattern engineering by optimising patterns for better fit and fabric utilisation. These technologies automate repetitive tasks and enhance the design process. Sustainability and Customisation : Modern software focuses on sustainability by minimising waste and allowing for personalised fit and design. These advancements contribute to more sustainable and customer-centric fashion production. Thus, the evolution of pattern-making techniques, with a focus on zero-waste design principles, has transformed the fashion industry. Today’s pattern-making blends traditional skills with modern technology. Computer-aided design (CAD) software has revolutionised the creation and adjustment of patterns, providing greater accuracy, scalability, and the ability to include intricate design details with ease. Additionally, 3D modelling has further advanced pattern-making by enabling designers to visualise garments in three dimensions, improving the overall design process. These innovations have significantly enhanced the accuracy and efficiency of garment construction, unlocking new opportunities for creativity and customisation. A major focus of modern pattern-making is sustainability. Designers are increasingly adopting zero-waste design methods to minimise textile waste and maximise fabric use. This approach not only reduces the environmental impact of the fashion industry but also supports ethical and responsible practices. New technologies, such as apps and 3D computing, help designers create more accurate and precise patterns while exploring innovative designs that were previously impossible with traditional methods. These techniques align with the growing demand for sustainable fashion, allowing for the creation of garments that are both aesthetically pleasing and eco-friendly. Advanced technology has also made it easier to integrate pattern pieces seamlessly, allowing fabrics to flow naturally with the body and enhancing the overall form of the garment. The adoption of zero-waste design principles has now become a part of fashion design education and production. Despite certain challenges, these new pattern-making techniques have revolutionised the fashion industry by promoting sustainability and creativity. They have improved the accuracy, efficiency, and customisation of garment construction, and in the process addressing environmental concerns and supporting ethical practices. Top Pattern-Making Software for the Apparel Industry Pattern-making plays a critical role in the apparel industry, translating design concepts into templates that guide garment production. With technological advancements, software tools now assist pattern makers, enhancing accuracy and efficiency. Below is an overview of the top pattern-making software available today. Gerber AccuMark – This is widely used for pattern creation, grading, and marker-making. It offers both 2D and 3D solutions and integrates advanced features like virtual prototyping, fabric optimisation, and automated nesting. Gerber AccuMark enhances productivity by reducing material waste and improving garment fit. It offers a range of products, including AccuMark 2D, 3D, and AccuNest, which together streamline the design and production process. Lectra Modaris – This company provides advanced 2D and 3D pattern-making solutions, widely used for its precision and efficiency. The software automates pattern adjustments, reducing manual work and offering intelligent design tools for pleating, grading, and fit verification. Its Modaris Expert version supports faster pattern development and improved collaboration through integrated systems. Lectra’s flexible pricing model makes it accessible for both large manufacturers and independent designers. Optitex – This software stands out with its realistic 3D simulations and seamless integration with Adobe Illustrator. It enhances fabric utilisation through advanced marker-making and nesting capabilities. The software’s O/Cloud system promotes collaboration and remote work, streamlining design sharing and communication across the supply chain. Optitex is known for its efficient pattern grading, 3D visualisation, and centralised data management, making it ideal for improving design accuracy and reducing waste. CLO 3D – This is a user-friendly software offering 3D garment visualisation, pattern-making, and material simulation. It allows designers to create, modify, and simulate garments with precision, ensuring accurate fit and design representation. CLO’s accessible pricing and continuous updates make it popular among fashion professionals, particularly for its realistic 3D draping and seamless integration with other design tools. Adobe Illustrator – Although not typically used for professional pattern-making, Adobe Illustrator is a favourite among home sewing enthusiasts. It is ideal for creating digital sewing patterns, offering vector editing and layering capabilities. While not compatible with large-scale production equipment, Illustrator is affordable and effective for hobbyists or small-scale designers. Modern Innovations in Pattern-Making for Clothes The fashion industry is undergoing a significant transformation with the introduction of advanced pattern-making and engineering tools. Innovations such as 3D simulations, AI-generated patterns, and laser cutting are reshaping how designers create garments, while also promoting sustainability. Let us explore these developments in detail. Digital Pattern Simulation One of the most notable advancements in pattern-making is the use of digital pattern simulation. Traditionally, designers created physical samples to test their designs, but now virtual prototypes are increasingly replacing these. Advanced software enables designers to create and view garments in a digital space, providing a realistic preview of how the garments will look and behave in real life. This significantly reduces the need for physical samples. CAD systems streamline the creation of patterns, making it easier for designers to experiment with different shapes and sizes. They also enhance collaboration within design teams by allowing everyone to work on the same digital platform. Another breakthrough is the integration of 3D simulation software, which allows for detailed and realistic garment visualisation. Designers can make adjustments in the digital environment, saving time and resources otherwise spent on physical prototypes. Scaling patterns for various sizes has also become more efficient with smart algorithms that adjust the base pattern automatically. These algorithms ensure consistency across all sizes, which is crucial for mass production. AI-Powered Pattern Generators AI is revolutionising pattern-making by analysing large datasets of body measurements and design preferences. AI algorithms can generate custom patterns that offer a more precise fit and enhanced personalisation. This technology caters to individual customers’ unique measurements, enabling the creation of garments that fit better and meet personal style preferences. Laser Cutting Technology Laser-cutting technology is replacing traditional pattern-cutting methods, offering precision and efficiency. Laser cutters handle intricate patterns with ease, reducing material waste and speeding up the production process. This method aligns with the growing emphasis on sustainable fashion, as it minimises waste and supports eco-friendly production practices. Thus, the evolution of pattern-making tools is significantly impacting the fashion industry. Digital simulations, AI, and laser cutting are streamlining design and production processes, reducing waste, and enhancing customisation. These innovations not only improve efficiency but also align with the industry’s increasing focus on sustainability. Embracing these technologies is crucial for designers and manufacturers who want to stay competitive and meet modern fashion demands. Benefits of Using Advanced Software As discussed in this article, advanced pattern engineering software provides numerous benefits for the apparel industry. Adopting these tools is a significant step towards enhancing productivity, accuracy, and overall quality. As technology continues to evolve, these tools are becoming more integral to the design and manufacturing processes, helping companies remain competitive and responsive to market demands. Automation and Efficiency : The shift from manual to automated pattern-making software is driven by the need for greater efficiency. These tools drastically reduce the time required to create patterns, speeding up the entire production process. Accuracy and Quality : Advanced pattern-making software ensures high accuracy in design, resulting in better-fitting garments. This precision minimises errors that often occur with manual drafting, leading to higher-quality end products. Cost Reduction : By minimising fabric wastage and reducing the need for extensive manual labour, these software solutions lower overall manufacturing costs. This cost efficiency is essential for staying competitive in the fast-paced apparel industry. Flexibility and Customisation : Modern pattern-making software allows for a high degree of customisation, enabling designers to easily modify patterns to meet specific customer requirements. This flexibility is crucial for brands looking to offer personalised and made-to-measure services. Integration with Other Systems : Many of these software tools integrate with other systems, such as production management and inventory control, and creating a seamless workflow from design to manufacturing. Sustainability : By optimising fabric usage and reducing waste, these technologies contribute to more sustainable production practices, aligning with the industry’s growing focus on environmental responsibility. Conclusion The evolution of pattern engineering software has fundamentally transformed the apparel industry, progressing from labour-intensive manual techniques to the use of sophisticated digital solutions. Initially, pattern-making relied on manual tools, which were time-consuming and prone to errors. The introduction of CAD systems revolutionised this process by enabling digital patterns, reducing drafting time, and enhancing accuracy. This advancement was further complemented by integrating CAD with CAM systems, which automated cutting and sewing, streamlining production. The rise of 3D pattern-making and virtual prototyping improved efficiency by allowing designers to visualise garments in three dimensions, reducing the need for physical prototypes. Cloud-based platforms enhanced collaboration and project management, while AI and machine learning optimised patterns for better fit and fabric utilisation. These innovations have led to significant benefits, including increased efficiency, reduced costs, higher-quality garments, and enhanced customisation. Most notably, they support sustainability by minimising fabric waste and promoting eco-friendly practices, marking a significant step towards a more innovative and responsible fashion industry. article_title: Learning From IT – Making Fashion Agile
sub_title: Read article about “The trouble with automation is that it often gives us what we don’t need at the cost of what we do”, Nicholas Carr, American journalist, Pulitzer Prize finalist and author of ‘Does IT matter’. and more articles about Textile industary at Fibre2Fashion
article_content: “The trouble with automation is that it often gives us what we don’t need at the cost of what we do”, Nicholas Carr, American journalist, Pulitzer Prize finalist and author of ‘Does IT matter’. While 21 st century’s radical technological shifts changed almost every sector and industry’s business as usual, many players operating in labour intensive industries with customised product offerings find it extremely difficult to adapt and leverage technological advancements to their full potential. Fashion houses too find themselves stuck in the middle, determining which technologies, solutions or tools are best suited to their existing operational practices and current business models. While organisations keep investing heavily in technologies and tools to make their processes agile, aiming to keep pace with the ever-changing competitive landscape, often, these technologies soon become dreary, unable to deliver any real advantage, and only bring more burden of documentation and reporting. How Industry Reacted to Tech Advancements in the Past? The transition started somewhere in the mid-2010s, with brands leveraging early versions of targeted solutions, including PLM modules, tech-pack builders and TNA trackers. However, due to high dissonance between skills of then existing manpower and relevant skillset required to leverage full potential of these tools, it narrowed the scope and daunted the pace at which these technologies were adapted. The entire value chain of suppliers, buyers, designers and retailers were still heavily dependent on data, which was managed and circulated in spreadsheets, causing data redundancy, data loss, delays, reworks and siloed data management practices. This bleak landscape started to look promising after emergence of SaaS and cloud technology, giving businesses much simpler, scalable, and implementable solutions. These solutions could now be customised to a business’s needs, were open to integrations with third parties, and were billed only on features selected. Manpower too was getting technology literate, given an imminent need of upskilling for both present and future. Implementation of best practices using ERP, CRM and SCM solutions became common, and many businesses started investing heavily to either build or sustain their competitive advantage through these technological advancements. COVID-19 outbreak, and subsequent lockdowns proved to be an inflection point and landed a big blow to the traditional way merchandising, buying, sourcing and designing operated. 3D modelling, virtual fit sessions, sample approvals, need for product cataloguing and building digital shelf became the new norms to operate. The Current Landscape Presently, with forever increasing technological layers over operations and mushrooming new solutions, businesses are carefully recalibrating their IT strategy to align technology to operational excellence and not vice-versa. However, in pursuit of keeping pace with recent technological advancements, managers often overlook the fact that they cannot leverage full potential of a solution unless they create complimentary changes in existing processes/interactions. The idea of implementing ERP or any solution is to leverage best practices it brings along, and not customise those solutions to existing internal practices. Oftentimes though, organisations fail to acknowledge this fact and create complex customisations to suit their business as usual. In their pursuit to become a technological leader, some businesses even keep switching between systems every couple of years, thereby paying huge indirect costs of training, switching, implementing and disruptions. This era of technological augmentation, where fashion businesses kept adding layers of technology over existing operations, has resulted in poor selection and integration of multiple systems. Many companies regularly face integration challenges between these systems, leaving their information vulnerable to attacks and data leaks. The underlying problem is the specialised nature of operations and customised solutions catering to individual functions. And hence functions (departments) have their own solutions which are integrated to a centralised ERP. CRM, PLM and CAD are some of these systems which fail to interact comprehensively with each other, and yet, are critical to their respective functions for BAU (Business As Usual). This complex landscape with multiple solutions, all having different touchpoints, oftentimes give mixed signals for various market changes and makes it difficult to clearly identify meaningful disruptions to chalk out action plans. Fashion businesses operating on long lead times and irreversible product line decisions are then caught off guard as they fail to respond on time, giving rise to price wars and wafer-thin margins for everyone operating in that segment. For example, a business witnessing muted topline growth may claim decrease in new customer enrolments through its CRM solution insights, but may simultaneously fail to marry it effectively with SKU level sales or design attributes to identify patterns of buying behaviour. It thus offers consumer promotions on enrolments, thereby marginally increasing conversions, but losing bottom-line and triggering price wars in the process. How to, then, end this vicious downward spiral and break free to create a new dimension of sustainable competitive advantage? How to make systems agile and how to create complementary practices to leverage full potential of solutions? The answer to these can be found looking outwards and gaining insights from industries which operate under similar dynamics. Learning it from IT In the present context, complimentary practices refer to building generic skills and processes between cross functional teams which help enable efficient collaboration without investing in implementation and training of a specialised nature. These practices aim to serve as a binding agent without disrupting existing solutions and their architecture. Creating complimentary practices helps a business develop sustainable advantage and leverage full potential of any existing/new solutions as this enables a function to focus on leveraging the specialised features and best practices of the solution instead of keeping tabs on data mismatch, data sufficiency and data reconciliation. This also helps chip away the bureaucratic layers from existing practices, making communications more transparent while simultaneously reducing reporting at each level. Neither these practices disrupt business as usual, nor do they open a separate communication channel. They can help build and sustain collaborative workflows and increase adaptation of best practices offered by IT solutions in a holistic way, giving various functions visibility to the outcome of siloed activities. These practices and tools which are heavily leveraged across IT, are built to support dynamic business requirements where every project is customised and is bound to follow a critical timeline to meet. By nature, and criticality, these projects require constant communication, task allocation, ownership, tracking, reporting and many other aspects which resemble fashion and retail BAUs. Though many apparel brands currently leverage these practices, they primarily brand them as IT practices and confine them to IT project management teams. Effortless in nature, they are powerful enough to bring a radical change to businesses without further burdening them with more complexities and costs. Four such practices/tools are listed below, which can bring agility to the processes and may help deliver competitive advantage to a business. As-is Analysis : As-is analysis is a powerful design thinking technique often leveraged in projects and process re-engineering to understand how the existing system behaves, maximising our understanding of the process from perspective of multiple stakeholders. This helps identify impediments, UDEs (Undesirable Entities), reworks and bottlenecks in a process, which then can further be used to recreate an optimised workflow without disrupting BAUs. It lays out the existing process in a connected workflow model, highlighting various nodes including start, decision, action, and end; thus, chalking out convergence and divergence of multiple flows, and clearly identifying UDEs and focus areas. Agile Project Management : Traditional seasonal planning in the apparel industry follows a waterfall approach, which entails linear, irreversible flow from planning to execution. It is much like a waterfall where water can only progress to the next level with little to no scope of fixing anything in phases which are already completed. Once planned, waterfall approach negates any scope of incorporating market feedback, business shifts or new requirements, and delivers what has been planned, making businesses vulnerable to any disruptions. Agile on the other hand, advocates a project management framework open to feedback and delivering value at the end of each sprint (A small time boxed event). This helps businesses to respond quickly to trends, competitor moves and any other disruption which may come as a surprise. This also helps eliminate process waste and reduces magnitude of failure. Zara is probably one of the examples of delivering fresh assortment every 3 weeks under operations which resemble agile principles closely. JIRA : JIRA is a tool used across the IT industry to manage projects, prioritise deliverables, assign tasks, raise issues, monitor progress, and build co-ordination between cross functional teams working together. It is a simple tool with intuitive UI, which does not require any technical expertise to operate. It reduces unnecessary documentation, promotes ownership of work and gives a holistic view of current progress to all stakeholders in a minimalist dashboard view. It helps to time stamp events, generate automated reports and set target vs expectations while enabling teams with self-organising. It reduces dependence on multiple communication channels, including emails, and notifies everyone on real time about status changes/issues/flags. These capabilities can heavily be leveraged in apparel industry where cross functional teams seek constant visibility on tasks from others, and getting a holistic view of progress consumes a significant amount of time and efforts. Scrum Teams : The concept of scrum teams highlights the essence of organising a small unit of cross functional individuals, assembled to deliver project goals. While traditionally apparel industry is structured in functions, the idea advocates forming specialised nuclear teams focused to deliver one objective only. Imagine a small unit of individuals comprising a designer, a merchandiser, a buyer and a technician working together to deliver a range of 50 designs. This team is managed by a ‘Scrum Master’, who acts as a servant leader, removing any impediments for the team, and lead by a ‘Product Owner’ who prioritises tasks and deliverables as per evolving business landscape. The whole team works together towards a single objective— to deliver 50 designs in the given timeframe, trimming any departmental bureaucracy, approval and communication. Conclusion While organisations keep pursuing excellence through building new layers of technology, these practices offer business agility within existing infrastructure and help build complimentary workflows for leveraging full potential of any solution. They offer making operations agile, with little process waste and drive productivity within teams with cross functional expertise (which oftentimes use different systems for their BAUs), helping reduce documentation, increasing ownership, and giving live monitoring to all the stakeholders. Traditionally branded as IT practices, these are essentially domain agnostic practices/tools which can be heavily leveraged within the apparel industry to make systems and teams handle disruptions and work closely to deliver value to the business, while simultaneously helping businesses generate more value from new/existing technology by focusing to adapt to best practices these solutions offer. article_content: Computers and textiles have become an important part of everyday life, say B Deepti Reddy , Ayodya Kavitha and Dr J Hayayadana . Once upon a time, and for centuries thereafter, computers did not have anything to do with textile production, especially handlooms. This was the era before computers developed and in the early decades of their existence. With increase in demand for textiles, use of computers in textile production has reduced time and effort taken to produce fabric and increased production. Technological developments have helped qualitative and quantitative changes in textiles. Computers are used for their speed, power and versatility. They facilitate quick computations and precise solutions, saving time. A set of instructions and procedures address the task to be performed, speeding up production and avoiding slower manual work. Computers are widely used in various departments of the textile industry. User-friendly operating systems in spinning: Most operations are controlled through user-friendly operating systems, such as push buttons, electronic screens and electronic stop motions. Electronic screens provide data such as number of bales plucked during a single passage, length of sliver in carding, controls of the machine to be conveyed to another worker and length and diameter of the yarn. Push buttons provide easy access to control the machine. Electronic stop motions stop the machine during any breakage, reducing losses.Touch screens are the most recent trend in operating these machines. Fig 1: Electronic screen on a carding machine showing sliver properties To analyse design and prepare peg plan Using a programme, one can develop a peg plan or card cutting plan providing pattern and loom specifications. This saves time and effort. Software creates the card cutting plan by clicking pictures of an object or a person. Fig 2: Computerised jacquard card punching machine Computerised jacquard loom Unlike older punch jacquard looms, electronic looms use computer generated files that lift threads to make a pattern entered into a computer. Each pixel represents one thread. The computer translates the design into instructions for the loom. A black dot lifts a warp thread or no hole is punched. White spaces represent warp threads to be left down or punch a hole. Electronic jacquard looms use computer-generated point papers to control the loom. This file is the source for modern card punching equipment. Fig 3: Computerised jacquard Computerised knitting machine Modern knitting machines knit a whole garment without cutting or sewing. Some designs may require partial stitching. Software converts the design into a code which the computer understands. The code is fed through a chip and the mechanisms are shown on an electronic screen so that the machine can communicate with the operator. The whole process, from casting on to casting off, to shaping and making many different types of stitches, is automated. The gauge and needle butts follow the path according to the instructions from the software to create the design. This allows faster knitting and higher productivity. Fig 4: Computerised knitting machine Testing Computers are principally used in testing to record and compute values. To record, values are transferred via analogue to digital form and displayed on the screen. Instruments like AFIS and HVI have this facility and error-free results are processed at a fast rate. These machines compute collected data and provide results of the test. They also store data and print it. The process is automated and can be repeated. Fig 5: Report showing test results for yarn count In wet processing Some mistakes were inevitable during wet processing. They could not be recognised or tested by humans. So, computers were brought in. Spectrophotometer: checks the shade of the dyed fabric Datacolour: for formation of accurate dye types Buffer Calculator: calculates amount of alkali/acid for the required buffer Fastnesss properties: computers check the fastness properties In printing, computers develop the designs and prepare screens which need accuracy like galvano and liquor screens. Digitised printing is the most happening segment in the vertical. Inkjet printing on fabric is also possible with an inkjet printer by using fabric sheets with removable paper backing. Creating patterns CAD/CAM technology is finding wide acceptance because of its immense use in design and development of textile machinery. CAD/CAM technology allows the user to design a product or a part of the product or even alter the product. The product can be viewed in 2D or 3D format. Parts of the machine like cams, tappets and the making of blue prints of the machines or parts of the machine. The efficiency and result of the altered part could also be tested in the software itself. Computers are also used to create the patterns for apparel and alter them with software like Richpeace and Tukatech . Fig 6: Pattern making software Fig 7: Designing a machine part using CAM Making markers A marker is a long, thin paper which contains of all necessary pattern pieces of different sizes of a particular garment. The pattern pieces should be arranged in such a way that there should be less fabric wastage. These patterns are arranged in various ways in the marker making software. The direction and position of pattern pieces could be rearranged a number of times, which is a tedious process if paper is used. The sizes can also be altered easily on a computer. Fig 8: Marker planning software Logo embroidery machine Most embroidery machines in the garment sector are controlled by computers. They work according to the pre-processing programmes given by the user. The instructions can be given through a USB or the machine can be connected directly to the system. The computer controls different motors which move the needle bar up and down and side by side, tensioning discs, feed dog and other elements in the machine. In single needle embroidery machines, the user changes thread colour. In multi-needle embroidery machines, the machine trims and changes thread colour according to programmed instructions. Popular software includes Bernina, Wilcom DecoStudio E3, and Embird Embroidery Studio Digitizing Software. Fig 9: Six-headed logo embroidery machine Software that repeats patterns on home textiles for apparel In home textiles, we often see patterns repeated. These patterns are placed at the required position using the software and then printed on the fabric. The positioning is exact, using grid lines. The design could be flipped horizontally, vertically or diagonally or repeated, since software offers flexibility. Software like Illustrator, Photoshop, Firework and Genue (for ipod) create and repeat patterns. Designing children's clothes with a 3-dimensional parametric dress form Infant garments cost more than adult garments because extra care is taken during their production as the patterns are small and seams should not be uncomfortable for the baby. So, it is necessary to give the manufacturer every minute detail such as stitch length, type of stitch, direction of stitch and patterning. For that, 3D patterns allow every part of the garment to be clearly visible and production is smooth. Fig 10: Conversion of 2D pattern to 3D Apparel Evolving IT trends for mass customisation in apparel industry Through E-commerce, products are reaching customers easily. Textiles are the top selling category in the E-commerce sector. Not only garments, even textile machinery is sold online. Even handloom products are available at the doorstep, unlike the previous scenario where the customer had to purchase the product at the manufacturing area. Success of sites like Jabong, Myntra and Snapdeal has encouraged India's leading textile manufacturer Arvind Ltd to start its own e-commerce site, Arvind Internet Ltd. Cloud computing in textiles Cloud computing or Internet-based computing provides data sharing to computers and other devices on demand. This has replaced the need to carry stacks of papers and files which could then be misplaced. Large files are transferred within minutes. The order quantity information, the CAD/CAM files, machinery guides, production planning files, raw material management and supply chain management are easily shared. However, cloud computing runs the risk of hacking, data loss and lack of control. Fig 11 Computers are used in process cycle management and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) The industry needs to keep up with developing technology. In the last few decades, many developments like automation in spinning, weaving and garmenting have taken place in the textile sector. The Information Technology (IT) revolution made things easier and faster. Using computers, the textile sector reached new heights. Computers are, in fact, the pointer to a more promising future. article_content: Pradeep Kulshrestha explains the benefits of direct creel in weaving. Conventional weaving was carried out by warp packages, beginning with warping-direct and sectional, then sizing, if required, and then on looms. But the process now has been modified, especially in technical textiles. It is simple and cost effective. Due to continuity of longer warp length through drum in running loom, loss of time in beam gaiting is fully avoided. Less contribution of skilled manpower also reduces the weaving cost with satisfactory production and product quality. The floor space depends on sorts to run on loom. Provisions for more than one type of warp packages to hold yarn or fibre can be made. This is very effective in saving costs and maintaining consistency in woven fabric productivity if the same product is running for longer time. Conventional warping process: For weaving, warp ends earlier came from direct creel or V-creel to wind on wrappers beam in direct warping and on weavers beam in sectional warping. These beams require beam gaiting on loom. Warping needed minimum one operator and a helper; beam gaiting required minimum three-beam gaiter, assistant and fitter. Six to eight looms were allocated to a team of weaver and helper. These seven skilled workers can now be replaced by a weaver and one or two helpers on loom if direct creel and drum weaving is carried out. Waste control: Due to continuity in weaving, much lesser quantity of warp waste is generated compared to weaving with weavers beam. In rapier looms, selvedge waste remains under norm (less than 3 per cent). Saving in time: Beam gaiting is not required, and therefore, a lot of time is saved, as there is no need to frequently reset loom and troubleshoot to repeatedly produce fabric without defects as per sample. Exhausted warp packages can be replaced during weaving by just applying knots at both ends. Scheduled maintenance: For exclusive cleaning and lubrication of loom, total packages on creel need to be changed, or else the warp packages can be changed intermittently without affecting loom functioning. Safety of creel: Creel is balanced by its own weight and the total weight of warp material kept on it. It is advisable to put foundation bolts as well as support from wall and pillars so that it may not fall down or vibrate with working loom. Even detachable racks should be joined together and can be separated, if required. Possibility of high efficiency: In fact the opportunity of process control during weaving is more in direct creel because an individual package can be replaced if it causes difficulty during weaving, but in beam, nothing can be done except compromising quality. Efficiency is not affected because of more beam preparation defects to rectify on loom or to compromise with loom working till beam finish. Many fabricators in India are making direct weaving creel at low investment to convert rapier and projectile weaving looms from 'beam to creel facility'. Replacement of weavers beam can be carried out by revolving the metallic drum. Fabricators are making creel for sectional warpers, direct warpers and beaming machines based on yarn or roving package type to be used. Different tensioners are available for each application-from finest polyester monofilament to coarse carbon fibre. Cost savings in fibre: If weaving of small-length fibre is required for composite research and applications, during initial rewinding from big warp package to small packages and at completion, pre-estimated other yarn of cheaper cost can be tied that will be wasted in process. Weaving options: For running Dyneema, various provisions using aramid, carbon, polypropylene, glass, etc are made to adjust the warp layer upon the drum. Even the same loom may be operated by creel-drum method or putting weavers beam on its bracket. For a range of weaving yarns , this provision is optional. In modern looms, drum and creel are not deteriorated through long term usage if scheduled maintenance and lubrication is conducted properly. Comparison of direct creel loom and loom working with beam: Conclusion: For continuous requirements of fabrics like carbon, aramid, glass, etc, direct creel is an appropriate process with loom for mass production. Even small quantity of costly fabric can be woven by rewinding the required number of warp packages from a few big packages. Power consumption is minimum because a number of equipment are limited with direct creel weaving technology. Furthermore, the versatility of the loom is an important factor, so that most fabrics can be woven as per changing requirements and trends. Looms are mostly equipped with microprocessor-based controls. Analysing their data and taking timely action will result in optimum productivity.
